CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.
Machine Learning.comment: 37 pages, including appendices and checklist. Code: https://github.com/Louiii/CES ; data and checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/datasets/lorob/CES

Machine Learning.title: Teaching LLMs to Recommend and Defer in Underrepresented Epilepsy Care
Machine Learning.summary: Specialist epilepsy expertise is scarce in resource-constrained settings. Clinical decision-support systems must adapt to local prescribing practices and recognize when specialist review is needed. We study pediatric epilepsy care in Uganda, predicting anti-seizure medication regimens from longitudinal clinic notes. General-purpose language models achieve non-trivial agreement with physician prescriptions, but neurologists' review reveals Western prescribing defaults that do not account for local practices. We introduce MANANA, a non-parametric prompt-learning framework that learns local prescribing guidance from a small patient-level training set. MANANA turns prescription errors into auditable prompt memory, with single-agent and multi-agent variants, and improves over classical ML models, direct LLM prompting, and prompt-optimization baselines across two independently collected Ugandan cohorts. The learned prompt trajectory also provides a basis for estimating uncertainty. Bayesian prompt averaging (BPA) combines predictions across this trajectory to produce prescription likelihoods and a deferral signal. Using the same MANANA-Multi trajectory, BPA improves top-1 physician-regimen agreement from 66% to 70% on Cohort A and from 73% to 75% on Cohort B while preserving top-3 coverage. On Cohort B, its most confident half of cases achieves 95% precision, and its most confident quarter achieves 99% precision, supporting deferral of lower-confidence cases for specialist review. These results suggest a path toward locally adapted clinical LLM systems that learn from limited site-specific data and focus scarce specialist attention on uncertain cases.

Machine Learning.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
Machine Learning.summary: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.

Machine Learning.title: Reasoning Reranking with Semantic IDs as the Sole Item Representation
Machine Learning.summary: Reasoning rerankers write a rationale before ranking a candidate slate, and existing systems read item metadata to do so, even though generative recommenders increasingly represent items as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs). Ranking from SIDs alone has two appeals: SID prompts are far shorter than the matched item text, and although item codes are fixed from content, the backbone learns their token embeddings in part from user-item interaction sequences, so the tokens can carry behavioral signal that item text lacks. That training targets next-item generation, and whether it supports ranking a supplied slate from SIDs alone is untested. We build ReRankID, a controlled testbed in which models reason and rank from a history and slate shown only as SIDs, varying item rendering, history length, and slate size one at a time. On this testbed, such models often copy the input order instead of reranking, and readable metadata does not repair the failure. We compare supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled self-training, on-policy distillation, and verifier-based reinforcement learning as post-training methods and find that they elicit the missing behavior. The strongest post-trained model, the 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward, gives the best SID-only ranking and matches strong text-reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer. It ranks above random with no history at all, where a caption-reading reference does not, and it keeps its gains at long histories, where text prompts pass 50k tokens and the caption-reading reference stops improving. In a paired rationale audit, this model argues trade-offs better than that reference but describes items less accurately. The common post-training methods we test thus elicit ranking from SIDs but not faithful item descriptions, which calls for post-training that improves the reasoning itself, not only the ranking it produces.

Machine Learning.title: Reinforcement Learning in MDPs with Information-Ordered Policies
Machine Learning.summary: Many operational Markov decision processes provide structured information where a trajectory generated under one policy may also reveal how other policies would have performed. We formalize this through an information order over a parameterized policy class, writing $π_{θ'} \preceq π_θ$ when data collected under $π_θ$ can be used to estimate the long-run average cost of $π_{θ'}$. We develop an epoch-based reinforcement learning algorithm for infinite-horizon average-cost MDPs with continuous state and action spaces that exploits this order through counterfactual inference. For a $d$-dimensional policy class whose information order has width $w$, the algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{wdT/α})$ regret relative to the optimal policy in the class, where $H$ is a bias span upper bound and $α$ denotes an "information ratio". Thus, the width captures the effective exploration complexity of the problem, interpolating between full counterfactual feedback and unstructured policy learning. We instantiate the framework in lost-sales inventory systems with positive lead times, dual-sourcing systems governed by dual-index policies, and queues with state-dependent service rates. These applications yield new regret guarantees without requiring global convexity of the average-cost function or specialized arrival-rate structure. Numerical experiments show that exploiting the information order substantially improves learning performance over existing general-purpose and problem-specific benchmarks.

Machine Learning.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
Machine Learning.summary: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132.

Machine Learning.title: Rethinking Negative Prompting for Concept Suppression: Unconditional Anchoring and Localized Guidance
Machine Learning.summary: Text-to-image diffusion models have rapidly transitioned from research prototypes to widely deployed tools. Along with their impressive capabilities, these models can also generate harmful or undesirable content (e.g., NSFW imagery), motivating practical mechanisms for removing such concepts. Negative prompting, which uses the negative-prompt prediction as the guidance anchor, is among the most widely used mechanisms for steering sampling trajectories away from unwanted concepts. However, for jailbreak prompts, it can fail in a regime we refer to as \emph{guidance collapse}, where the model's denoising predictions for the prompt and negative prompt become similar, so that the guidance difference driving negative prompting vanishes and the guided prediction degenerates to the negative-prompt prediction, undermining suppression. To fix this issue, we propose TraSCE (Trajectory Steering for ConcEpt Suppression), a training-free inference-time method that makes negative prompting reliable under guidance collapse. TraSCE combines two complementary components: (i) unconditional anchoring, which makes the fallback under guidance collapse a neutral unconditional prediction rather than the negative-prompt prediction, and (ii) an alignment-localized steering step, which deliberately induces this collapse for adversarial prompts and steers the sample to the unconditional fallback, while remaining minimally intrusive on benign prompts. We evaluate TraSCE on adversarial prompt benchmarks targeting nudity and violence, and further demonstrate its applicability to suppressing artistic styles and objects. Across these settings, TraSCE substantially improves the robustness of negative prompting to jailbreak prompts without any training, weight updates, or pre-collected concept-specific data (prompts or images), while keeping the impact on general image quality small.

Machine Learning.title: Next Token or Vector? Learning How Far to Decode
Machine Learning.summary: Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, even when several upcoming tokens can be predicted together. We propose CADENCE (Context-Adaptive DEcoding), a generation method that learns both what to draft and how far to draft. Gaussian prediction heads represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, and a shared decoder converts the selected vector into token predictions in parallel. A learned router selects the prediction length from the model's own hidden states and predicted Gaussian parameters, adapting generation granularity to the current context with single-token generation as a fallback. The backbone verifies each proposed continuation and retains the prefix that matches its greedy predictions. Experiments with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval show that router-selected positions yield higher draft acceptance than applying the corresponding prediction length everywhere. CADENCE achieves up to 1.3x higher generation throughput than standard greedy decoding.

Machine Learning.title: TargetSEC: Plug-and-Play In-the-Wild Speech Emotion Conversion via Arousal-Conditioned Latent Style Diffusion
Machine Learning.summary: Speech Emotion Conversion (SEC) aims to transform the emotion of a source utterance into a target emotion while preserving content and speaker identity. SEC on in-the-wild data is challenging due to the non-parallel nature of training data and complex real-world acoustics. Existing fixed-duration approaches either struggle to shift the emotion effectively (high quality, low conversion) or degrade speech naturalness (low quality, high conversion). We propose TargetSEC, an embedding-driven latent diffusion framework that generates emotion-focused style embeddings conditioned on speaker identity and continuous emotion. Unlike methods that diffuse over spectrograms, TargetSEC operates in a compact latent space. Experiments on the MSP-Podcast dataset show that TargetSEC outperforms current non-duration baselines and matches or exceeds the duration-prediction baseline in conversion MSE and naturalness without explicit temporal modeling. Demo and code available at.

Machine Learning.title: Is the Policy Gradient a Gradient?
Machine Learning.summary: The policy gradient theorem describes the gradient of the expected discounted return with respect to an agent's policy parameters. However, many policy gradient methods omit the outer discount factor, yielding an update that need not equal the gradient of the discounted objective. Is the resulting update the gradient of another objective? This has been an open question for several years, and this lack of theoretical clarity has led to an abundance of misstatements in the literature. We answer this question for the resulting episode-summed, on-policy update by proving that it need not equal the gradient of any function. Further, we construct a counterexample in which exact expected updates drive the policy toward a deterministic limit that is globally pessimal with respect to both the discounted and undiscounted objectives, while the parameter diverges. We motivate this work by surveying the literature and showing that there remains a widespread misunderstanding regarding discounted policy gradient methods, with errors present even in highly-cited papers published at top conferences.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages. Corrections and clarifications to mathematical statements, Figure 1, and discussion of prior work; main result and original counterexamples retained

Machine Learning.title: Anytime Contracts for AI Services
Machine Learning.summary: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

Machine Learning.title: M$^2$RNN: Non-Linear RNNs with Matrix-Valued States for Scalable Language Modeling
Machine Learning.summary: Transformers are highly parallel but are limited to computations in the TC$^0$ complexity class, excluding tasks such as entity tracking and code execution that provably require greater expressive power. Motivated by this limitation, we revisit non-linear Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for language modeling and introduce Matrix-to-Matrix RNN (M$^2$RNN): an architecture with matrix-valued hidden states and expressive non-linear state transitions. We demonstrate that the language modeling performance of non-linear RNNs is limited by their state size, and show how the state size expansion mechanism enables efficient use of tensor cores. Empirically, M$^2$RNN achieves perfect state tracking generalization at sequence lengths not seen during training. These benefits also translate to large-scale language modeling. In hybrid settings that interleave recurrent layers with attention, Hybrid M$^2$RNN outperforms equivalent Gated DeltaNet hybrids by $0.4$-$0.5$ perplexity points on a 7B MoE model, while using $3\times$ smaller state sizes for the recurrent layers. Notably, replacing even a single recurrent layer with M$^2$RNN in an existing hybrid architecture yields accuracy gains comparable to Hybrid M$^2$RNN with minimal impact on training throughput. Further, the Hybrid Gated DeltaNet models with a single M$^2$RNN layer also achieve superior long-context generalization, outperforming state-of-the-art hybrid linear attention architectures by up to $8$ points on LongBench. Together, these results establish non-linear RNN layers as a compelling building block for efficient and scalable language models.

Machine Learning.title: Horizon-Aware Early Event Prediction for Tokamak Disruption Alarms
Machine Learning.summary: Disruption predictors must warn the plasma control system early enough for the intended response, and the required warning time differs between mitigation and avoidance. We view a warning system as a predictor that outputs a disruption risk and an alarm policy that acts on it, and ask which risk the predictor should learn. Binary classifiers do not specify when a disruption occurs, and survival analysis models the full distribution of the time to disruption, whereas an alarm depends only on the risk within a finite horizon. We introduce two horizon-focused targets into tokamak disruption prediction: a horizon-truncated survival objective and fixed-horizon early event prediction (EEP) with temporal label smoothing (TLS). We compare them with binary classification and survival analysis on the DIII-D, Alcator C-Mod, and EAST databases of DisruptionBench, evaluating the risk by its threshold-free ranking at a 40 ms deadline and the alarm policy by thresholds calibrated on validation data. On every device, TLS outperforms the deep survival models in both ranking and alarm performance; TLS performs best on DIII-D and EAST, and a random forest trained on a hard horizon target performs best on C-Mod. TLS also improves the calibrated alarm performance over hard targets placed at either end of its smoothing range on all devices, isolating the benefit of label smoothing. Horizon truncation alone did not consistently improve survival analysis. Alarm performance remains limited on C-Mod and DIII-D and varies strongly across training seeds, and ablations show that the target should extend to the required warning time.

Machine Learning.title: Reusing Calibration Gains across Model Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.

Machine Learning.title: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer
Machine Learning.summary: Similarity scores are often offered as evidence that a model shares structure with the brain or across languages. We ask what such a score reads when that structure is removed, or when the instrument measuring it does not work, in two settings. Across seventeen languages, a grammaticality probe transfers worse between more distant languages (r = -0.66). But the probe's own accuracy falls along the same axis and is at chance in four languages, four of the five most distant. Dropping them halves the explained variance, and because it also narrows the range of distances, the design cannot say how much of the gradient is the instrument. Counting the 272 language pairs as independent gives p = 0.0006 for a steering effect that is null when the seventeen languages are the unit (p = 0.155). In brain alignment, a training objective raises a language model's similarity to fMRI responses from 0.10 to 0.34 (reliability ceiling 0.54), yet targets with the brain correspondence destroyed still reach 0.31. A shuffled target scores about k/n against the real one, for rank k and n sentences, a baseline that can be computed before any model is trained. Both interventions work, yet we detect no distance-graded steering effect and no syntactic benefit from alignment. Before reading a correspondence score, measure how much of it survives without the correspondence.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 - Linguistic Principles for Foundation Models (LP4FM). Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/score-is-not-the-structure - revised to add more relevant references

Machine Learning.title: Unit-level aggregation breaks coverage in causal foundation models
Machine Learning.summary:
Causal foundation models (CFMs) show promising results for treatment-effect estimation, with unit-level estimates that are competitive on standard benchmarks. Many causal analyses, however, inform decisions through effects averaged over groups of units, such as the full sample, the treated units, or a subgroup, and for such decisions a CFM is useful only if its credible intervals are calibrated. We examine these intervals and find that their coverage degrades, both in simple synthetic settings and on standard benchmarks. On ACIC 2016, for example, temperature-calibrated 95% intervals from CausalPFN fall below nominal coverage beyond groups of 30 out of 4802 units, and intervals for the full-sample average contain the true value in only 20% of datasets.
  We trace this problem to how these models are trained and how their intervals are formed. They output a predictive distribution for one unit at a time and, at inference time, combine the unit-level variances as if the errors on different units were independent. We show formally that posterior uncertainty over the data-generating process makes these errors correlated. As a result, the combined variance is too small by a factor that grows with the size of the group. Empirically, this factor predicts where coverage fails and by how much. We then show that two neural process models, which make joint predictions for a group of units, account for this correlation and substantially improve coverage on synthetic tasks and, as heads on a frozen CausalPFN, on all six benchmarks.

Machine Learning.title: One Communicator, Three Vendors: Extending the MoA Predictive Theory to a Real NVIDIA+AMD+CPU MPI Ensemble
Machine Learning.summary: The companion MPI-extension paper validated the first communication-bearing machine-shape ensemble: four NVIDIA A100 ranks and four CPU ranks on one NCSA Delta node under one Open MPI job, reassembled by MPI_Gatherv. This paper extends it to a multi-vendor communicator. A Slurm heterogeneous job spanning Delta's A100 and AMD MI100 partitions places A100, MI100 and CPU ranks (nine in all) under one communicator for the first time. We give the theory (a w_i proportional to 1/t_i weight split for three concurrent realizations; a het-job specification as an admissible directive) and report real results, including what the run exposed: the 1/t split assumes time linear in rows, and this fails for the MI100 rank (6 rows took 597 ms against a linear prediction of 1.6 ms). A launch-geometry model, with predictions recorded before measuring, succeeds for the A100 (time flat from 128 to 3456 rows, stepping at exactly 3520 and 6976) and places the MI100 floor in the key loop; changing its launch settings cut about 600 ms to 14.6 ms and the energy per call at 6 rows by 32x, though the MI100 remains about 95x slower than an A100 at 8192 rows. Controlled reruns show that the companion paper's 8.1x A100 result and 22 ms Gatherv were artifacts of four ranks sharing one GPU under Open MPI's default transport. A key/value-split partition whose message sizes are derived from shapes alone is then run: the ring Allreduce of the 8.5 MB message took 11.3, 16.0 and 15.3 ms against a predicted 11-12 ms, the small Allreduce missed its prediction in every run, and compute times reproduce to about 1% while communication times vary up to 4x between runs. Each idea is introduced with a figure and closed with worked examples.

Machine Learning.title: Acquisition Function-Guided Generation for Bayesian Optimization over Discrete Spaces
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) over discrete spaces is challenging due to missing gradients and the sparsity of valid solutions. Latent-space BO sidesteps both issues by fitting a surrogate in the latent space of a generative model, which however substantially complicates the direct incorporation of domain knowledge that is naturally expressed in the original discrete space. In this work, we instead combine a pretrained generative model with a surrogate defined directly in data space, where inductive biases such as domain-specific kernels can be readily incorporated. Rather than maximizing the acquisition function over the discrete design space, our method samples candidates from the generative model under a distribution tilted by the acquisition function. To recover useful gradients for sampling, we embed this tilted distribution into a diffusion bridge that yields a smooth, posterior-averaged acquisition function. This leads to \emph{acquisition function guided generation} (AFGG), which we instantiate with a categorical diffusion model and an autoregressive normalizing flow. Across a broad suite of molecular benchmarks, the diffusion model variant performs on par with leading BO methods, while the flow model variant outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most cases and remains highly competitive otherwise. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/afgg.

Machine Learning.title: Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields for Rigid-Body Motion and Manipulation Planning
Machine Learning.summary: Rigid-body motion planning is fundamental to robotic transport and manipulation, where both object position and orientation determine whether a body can move through cluttered environments. This coupling makes planning chal- lenging because translation and rotation can be constrained very differently by surrounding geometry. We propose Shape- Aware Neural Time Fields, a physics-informed neural motion planning framework that learns a reusable travel-time, or cost- to-go, representation for rigid-body motion while explicitly accounting for these distinct geometric restrictions. The learned field captures local motion difficulty in translation and rotation and is paired with a sampling-based planner that balances progress toward the goal with the cost of reaching nearby poses. We evaluate the framework across 2D and 3D rigid- body planning tasks and non-prehensile manipulation through object pushing in diverse environments. Results show substantial improvements in planning success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural planning baselines, while remaining competitive with classical sampling-based planners at significantly lower planning times. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of both the learned representation and the proposed planning strategy. Finally, closed-loop pushing experiments under execution deviations and external disturbances demonstrate that fast replanning enables reactive and adaptive task execution.

Machine Learning.title: PAC Learning with Query Feedback
Machine Learning.summary: We study realizable multiclass PAC learning with query feedback, where each training example provides a single binary response indicating whether its true label belongs to a chosen subset from a fixed query family. Our main contribution is the query dimension, a combinatorial parameter that captures both the structure of the hypothesis class and the ability of the available queries to distinguish labels. This parameter generalizes the bandit DS dimension, which it recovers under singleton queries. We establish a sample-complexity lower bound of $Ω(D/\varepsilon)$ and an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(D^2/\varepsilon)$, suppressing factors polylogarithmic in the number of labels and the failure probability. When the available queries can split every candidate set into two parts of comparable size, we improve the upper bound to $\widetilde{O}(D/\varepsilon)$, yielding a characterization up to logarithmic factors.

Machine Learning.title: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL
Machine Learning.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning, in which an LLM judge scores responses against prompt-specific criteria, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks without verifiable answers. The rubric, however, is only a proxy for response quality, and a policy trained against it long enough learns to exploit the difference. We train models with GRPO on medical and science rubrics and grade their responses on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks throughout training with two judges: the training judge and a stronger OOD judge. The two scores first rise together and then diverge. The policy is learning to satisfy the training judge without writing better responses, which is a form of reward hacking. To mitigate it, we propose Rubric Dropout, which applies dropout to rubric criteria: at each training step, a random subset of each rubric's criteria is removed from the reward, so the rewarded subset of criteria is resampled at each step. All responses sampled for the same prompt are scored on the same subset, so their rewards remain comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. We also introduce Block Dropout, which drops semantically similar criteria together so that a near duplicate of a dropped criterion cannot keep rewarding the same behavior. Across both benchmarks and models from 1.7B to 8B, dropout improves the gold judge's score on OOD benchmarks by up to 3 percent on HealthBench-Hard and 7 percent on ResearchQA, and it reduces both the gap between the two judges and over-crediting. It keeps in-domain reward close to the baseline, and dropout rates of 30-50 percent work best. Block Dropout improves the gold judge's OOD score further at the same dropout rate. Changing which criteria are rewarded at each step is a simple, inexpensive way to make rubric rewards harder to exploit.

Machine Learning.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention
Machine Learning.summary: A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. Existing time-series foundation models address these only in part, since they isolate each series or visit the two grid relations in separate blocks, and they fix the horizon and resolution before training begins. We introduce Morpheus-2.0, a compact encoder-only foundation model that represents targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid. Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.
Machine Learning.comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 16 tables. Aakriti and Manoj Cherukumalli contributed equally

Machine Learning.title: Latent State Utilization in Probabilistic Circuits
Machine Learning.summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are generative models that support efficient probabilistic inference. Adding latent states to a PC increases its representational capacity, but yields diminishing gains in likelihood. We use mutual information to examine how the dependence represented by a trained PC changes with latent size. Experiments with Hidden Chow-Liu Trees (HCLTs) on ImageNet32 show that learned dependence grows slowly and remains well below both the latent-state upper bound and estimates of dependence in the data. To understand how learning uses these states, we examine how strongly each sample favors particular latent states and how broadly states are used across the dataset. Tracking these measurements during HCLT training distinguishes rapid early posterior concentration from the more gradual stabilization of sample-dependent state preferences. Early measurements also guide initialization selection in HCLTs and hidden Markov models (HMMs), as well as tree selection in HCLTs. The resulting choices improve the ultimate performance across the tested latent sizes, providing a practical benefit from our study of latent-state utilization.

Machine Learning.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
Machine Learning.summary: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

Machine Learning.title: Learning Administrative Boundary-Aware Location Encoders via Reverse Geocoding
Machine Learning.summary: Location encoders learn compact representations of latitude--longitude coordinates for downstream geospatial prediction tasks. Existing approaches are pretrained using continuous or naturally occurring supervision, such as imagery, climate variables, or species distributions, and therefore do not explicitly capture administrative boundaries or place names, despite their strong influence on many real-world geospatial phenomena. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first method for learning administrative boundary-aware location encoders, using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal. Our approach can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their downstream performance. We further introduce RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture tailored to reverse-geocoding supervision, which yields additional gains and exceeds contemporary location encoders on several downstream tasks. Finally, the use of human-interpretable reverse-geocoded strings and residual-quantized semantic IDs provides a more interpretable representation of geographic location than existing approaches. Code and model weights to be released soon.

Machine Learning.title: Muon Operates Beyond the Edge of Stability
Machine Learning.summary: We study the Muon optimizer using sharpness and provide the first empirical evidence that the Flat Minima Hypothesis also applies to Muon. Further, we derive Muon's implicit preconditioner to analyze its potential Edge of Stability behavior. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show sharpness strongly correlates with generalization gap within each optimizer (Pearson $r = 0.45$-$0.69$, $p \leq 10^{-4}$), confirming the hypothesis holds for Muon similarly to Adam and SGD. However, Muon operates above the classical sharpness-based Adaptive Edge of Stability threshold that bounds diagonally-preconditioned optimizers like Adam and RMSprop, yet remains stable. Our findings suggest Muon operates in a fundamentally different regime than diagonally-adaptive methods. Defining the exact stability boundary for Muon remains an open question. All code is available at https://github.com/NikoCovic/DL-project.

Machine Learning.title: Finite-Sample Wasserstein Error Bounds and Concentration Inequalities for Nonlinear Stochastic Approximation
Machine Learning.summary: Stochastic approximation methods such as stochastic gradient descent and temporal-difference learning return either the last iterate or the Polyak--Ruppert average. We establish finite-sample Wasserstein-$p$ Gaussian approximation bounds for both outputs under a common framework combining moment bounds for the normalized iterates with quantitative Gaussian approximation of the appropriately weighted driving noise. These bounds yield convergence of admissible moments and high probability bounds with Gaussian leading terms: heavier dependence on the confidence level is confined to a correction that vanishes with the sample size. We verify the framework's conditions for nonlinear stochastic approximation with independent or Markovian observations and linear stochastic approximation with Markovian observations, with applications to stochastic gradient descent and temporal-difference learning.

Machine Learning.title: Torch-DPhys: A Torch-Native, MOOSE-Compatible Framework for Differentiable Physics Simulation and Hybrid Machine Learning Integration
Machine Learning.summary: We present Torch-DPhys, a Torch-native framework implemented in PyTorch for differentiable physics simulation and hybrid physics-machine learning. It implements selected thermal-hydraulic modeling concepts and discretizations from MOOSE's Thermal Hydraulics Module and the System Analysis Module (SAM), with a preliminary extension to continuum mechanics. Native tensor residuals support CPU and GPU execution, compilation of selected numerical kernels, and sparse direct linear solves. Sensitivities are obtained by differentiating executed numerical operations or through discrete adjoints of converged residual equations. Verification combines analytical solutions, reference-code comparisons, and derivative checks. Demonstrations cover plane-strain elasticity, one- and two-loop thermal-hydraulic transients, and an axisymmetric molten-salt fast reactor. For the reactor, comparison with SAM-Lite gives a maximum normalized field discrepancy of 1.13 x 10^-5 over 200 adaptive time steps, demonstrating agreement between the tested discrete implementations. Selected transient sensitivities are assessed using tangent-linear calculations and finite differences on fixed time schedules. Two applications illustrate the framework's connection between simulation and optimization. A residual-adjoint parameter-identification calculation recovers nominal pump head and heating power with relative errors below 0.06% from noiseless synthetic MOOSE observations. A separate three-loop plant demonstration uses solver-in-the-loop training of a predictive controller by differentiating trajectory-level objectives through the thermal-hydraulic simulation. These examples illustrate a foundation for gradient-based inference, control, and coupled physics-machine learning models in nuclear engineering.

Machine Learning.title: Upgrade the Retriever First: What an LLM Call per Chunk Buys in RAG
Machine Learning.summary: Many RAG pipelines pay one LLM call per chunk at indexing time to add titles, summaries, keywords and questions (enrichment) or document context (contextual retrieval, CR). We ask what that call buys over free structure and a better retriever. Our advice: upgrade the retriever first, chunk at headers, and enrich mainly for lexical retrieval. Under a plan made public before any index was built, 7B enrichment beats a free section-path prefix under a hybrid retriever by +5.5 recall points on Qasper; on FreshStack its gain (+2.7) does not survive Holm adjustment. It is equivalent to CR, which sends 5.8-8.7 times the input tokens, and Qasper answer F1 (7B reader) is equivalent for both contrasts. Header-led chunks beat 512-character windows; on FreshStack they lose to overlapping 256-token windows. Under qwen3-embedding and a reranker, the two strongest of eight retrievers (named as secondary before any outcome was computed), the CIs of 7B enrichment against the free prefix fall within the equivalence margins; under BM25 it gains +8.7. Exploratory analyses attribute the hybrid gain to document expansion and to repairing an untuned rank fusion; the free prefix under either strong retriever beats hybrid enrichment by +3.4 to +6.3 points, though the best 120B-indexed configuration leads the best free one by +2.5 on Qasper. Add-ons built on the call do no better than LLM-free controls, and late chunking lowers Qasper recall. We release the plan, harness and per-question results.
Machine Learning.comment: 29 pages (8-page main text). v4: confirmatory study with a plan made public before any index was built (951 Qasper and 235 FreshStack questions, eight retrievers). Results of v1-v2 are withdrawn (Appendix P). Code and data: https://github.com/bhavik-mangla/MDKeyChunker

Machine Learning.title: Predicting CVSS and CWE from CVE Descriptions with Fine-Tuned Small Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vector precisely for only 3.4% of CVEs. However, deriving scores from predicted vectors boosts the critical recall of TF-IDF logistic regression from 50.7% to 73.3% with no additional cost. And since the errors of the fine-tuned model and TF-IDF affect different CVEs, at least one system matches the correct severity tier for 75.8% of test CVEs.

Machine Learning.title: Constructive Universal Approximation by Infinite-Dimensional Neural Networks via Gaussian-Weighted Ridgelet Transform
Machine Learning.summary: Neural networks whose inputs are functions, as in operator learning, are usually shown to be universal by existence arguments, either by reduction to finite-dimensional networks or by Stone--Weierstrass-type density; these prove that approximants exist but say little about how the parameters depend on the target. We take a constructive route. We extend the ridgelet transform, an integral transform related to the Fourier, Radon, and wavelet transforms, to continuous maps on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, replacing the Lebesgue measure that is unavailable in infinite dimensions by Gaussian weights with a homogeneous mixture on the direction space. The resulting transform has a Plancherel identity and reconstruction formulas incorporating the frame operator, the correction induced by the weights, and it assigns to each target an explicit coefficient measure, one for every admissible analysis filter. From these representations we obtain uniform approximation on compact sets for all continuous non-polynomial activations of polynomial growth, including ReLU, and, by Monte Carlo sampling of the coefficient, finite-width networks with a dimension-free $O(N^{-1/2})$ error in the width $N$ for globally Lipschitz activations and coefficients with finite variation and second moments. Explicit examples include Gaussian targets and neural-operator layers. A companion Lean~4 formalization provides machine-checked proofs, with its correspondence to the manuscript documented at https://shosonoda.github.io/lean-operator-ridgelet/ .

Machine Learning.title: Inducing Fourier Geometry: A Smoothness Prior Imposes Approximate Translation Equivariance in Multimodal Stellar Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary: Learned representations often contain geometric structure induced by symmetries in the underlying data. We ask whether a known continuous parameter space can instead be used to \emph{induce} such structure when the corresponding symmetry is only approximate. We introduce a graph-Laplacian smoothness prior that encourages representations to vary smoothly over a physical parameter space without specifying a representation geometry; in the continuum limit it selects Laplacian eigenfunctions and therefore predicts the Fourier-like geometry associated with translation symmetry. On multimodal stellar representations spanning six astronomical surveys, the prior induces Toeplitz Gram structure and sinusoidal modes along stellar parameters, including in modalities whose native representations lack this geometry, while modality-specific residuals preserve structure outside the imposed coordinates. Of the exact-symmetry predictions, stationarity in a recoverable warped coordinate survives; diagnostics assuming exact quantization or asymptotic rates do not. The prior also improves downstream linear-probe performance and label efficiency, suggesting a general strategy: where a meaningful continuous parameter space exists, its local geometry can serve as a data-informed prior.

Machine Learning.title: An important Bottleneck in LLM Optimizers: Principle-Level Local Optima
Machine Learning.summary: Feedback-driven LLM optimizers are increasingly used for evolutionary search, Bayesian optimization, heuristic design, and scientific discovery. Yet rapid initial gains often give way to prolonged plateaus despite substantial remaining evaluation budgets. We investigate \emph{principle-level search collapse}, where an optimizer's search becomes confined to a narrow set of design principles, even though it may continue to generate distinct candidates and achieve small improvements. We assemble a diagnostic benchmark spanning molecular optimization, network sentinel-node selection, and GPU-kernel optimization, and introduce a decision-tree protocol combining principle narrowing, prolonged performance plateaus, and gaps to attainable reference solutions. Across 161 assessable runs on the three problem domains, 78.3\% receive support for collapse, including 55.3\% with strong support. Candidate-level variation can nevertheless conceal restricted search at the principle level. We then test \emph{diversity injection}, a common response to search stagnation, such as higher t, multiple LLMs, and web search, and show that it provides limited and inconsistent benefits: among 65 molecular runs, still 73.8\% and 53.8\% receive support and strong support respectively. We finally test reference-principle interventions and find that they improve some runs, but their benefits vary across models and tasks: access to a better principle does not guarantee its effective use. Our benchmark and diagnostic protocol provide a basis for evaluating future optimizers on principle-level collapse. Our findings highlight the need for online collapse detection and better mechanisms for generating and maintaining alternative principles during optimization.

Machine Learning.title: BanglaShield: A Script-Robust Safety Classifier and Benchmark for Bangla Native, Romanized, and Code-Mixed Prompts
Machine Learning.summary: Safety classifiers for large language models (LLMs) are typically built and evaluated on standard-script text, yet Bangla, like many lower-resource languages, is routinely written in native script, in Latin-script romanization, and code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. We introduce BanglaShield, a resource and model for graded prompt-safety classification across these written forms. We consolidate 10,245 Bangla prompts from six sources under a four-level taxonomy (Safe, Offensive, Harmful, Severe) and render each prompt in three aligned forms that share labels and a group-aware split, enabling strictly paired comparisons. Benchmarking six contemporary LLMs, including a Bangla-specialized one, on 36,882 classification queries and 24,318 judged responses, we find that LLM classifiers label 47.0% of unsafe native-script prompts as Safe, rising to 63.4% under romanization, while response-level safety accuracy drops by 10.3 points. Three multilingual guard models also pass 30.3-57.3% of unsafe native-script prompts. Using a model's own classification as an input filter reduces harmful compliance by only about five points. In contrast, BanglaShield, a compact fine-tuned encoder, reaches 87.8 macro-F1 on native-script and 84.4 on romanized prompts, outperforming the best LLM on each form by 42.8-46.1 points with ~130x fewer parameters than Gemma 4 31B. We release the corpus, splits, judgments, and model.

Machine Learning.title: When Clean Data Hurts: Learning with Monotone Corruptions Beyond Binary Classification
Machine Learning.summary:
Optimal learners are tailored to exploit the i.i.d.\ data assumption underlying the classic PAC model. What if an i.i.d.\ training sample were corrupted with correctly labeled examples drawn from an otherwise unrelated, even adversarial source? This model of learning with monotone adversarial corruptions was recently introduced by Larsen et al. (2026), who demonstrated that all known optimal binary learners suffer increased error rates in this setting, from $O(d / n)$ in the PAC model to $Ω(d \log(n / d) / n)$ under monotone corruption. Mehrotra (2026) proved this logarithmic factor to be necessary for binary classification, but left open the consequences of corruption for more general learning settings, such as multiclass classification and partial binary concept classes.
  As our primary result, we demonstrate that monotone adversaries are frighteningly more powerful in each of these settings. We exhibit a learnable multiclass problem, of DS dimension only 2, that becomes altogether unlearnable under a monotone adversary, and show an analogous result for partial binary concept classes. These results are achieved by an adaptive adversary permitted to view the original i.i.d.\ training set $S$ and to insert $b < \infty$ corrupted datapoints into $S$. In the multiclass example, the adversary need only insert a linear number $b = |S| = n$ of datapoints.
  We complement these impossibility results by proving that every class remains learnable when the number of adaptive additions is $o(n)$, which our previous multiclass lower bound proves to be tight. We further observe that the classic multiclass error rate of $O(d_{\mathrm{DS}} / n)$ remains achievable against adaptive adversaries restricted to a known constant budget $b = O(1)$, against semi-adaptive adversaries viewing only a $p$-fraction of $S$ for $p \in (0, 1)$, and against oblivious adversaries that cannot view $S$.

Machine Learning.title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models
Machine Learning.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black-box APIs and trained on large collections of real-world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre-training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre-training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black-box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state-of-the-art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre-training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.

Machine Learning.title: D-STEER: Two-Way Control of DPO-Induced Safety Behavior in Activation Space
Machine Learning.summary: Preference-based post-training shapes language-model behavior, but safer outputs do not reveal how that change is represented internally or how firmly it persists under direct intervention. This matters for open-weight models, where an actor with white-box access can manipulate internal representations at inference without touching parameters. Using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), we ask whether the safety behavior it introduces becomes deeply embedded or stays accessible to targeted activation-space interventions. We introduce D-STEER, an audit of two matched instruction-tuned and harmlessness-DPO pairs: OpenHermes-2.5-Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B OpenHermes. D-STEER derives layer-local directions from differences in matched prompt activations, adds them to the instruction-tuned model to install the DPO-associated safety change and subtracts them from the DPO model to remove it, with separate operating windows distinguishing behavioral control from degradation. On held-out HarmfulQA, all four interventions shift harmful enablement as intended and exceed norm-matched random controls; Mistral installation recovers 98% of the endpoint gap and the other three arms recover 46-50%. The intended direction transfers to HH-RLHF and AdvBench under frozen coefficients, although usable operating windows do not transfer universally. An independently rebuilt implementation reproduces the bidirectional pattern on the Mistral pair under different construction and intervention choices. A meaningful component of DPO-induced safety behavior therefore remains controllable through compact inference-time intervention, with the extent depending on the checkpoint pair and the steering implementation.
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, including supplementary material. Substantially revised manuscript with expanded experimental evaluation and methodological details; updated title, author list, affiliations and references

Machine Learning.title: UNO: Unlearning via Orthogonalization in Generative models
Machine Learning.summary: As generative models become increasingly powerful and pervasive, the ability to unlearn specific data due to privacy concerns, legal requirements, or harmful content has become increasingly important. Unlearning aims to selectively remove the influence of particular data without costly retraining from scratch. Effective unlearning requires (i) forgetting undesired data, (ii) preserving generation quality, (iii) retaining the influence of desired training data on model parameters, and (iv) computational efficiency. We propose fast unlearning algorithms based on loss gradient orthogonalization for unconditional and conditional generative models. We consider the loss function of the original model restricted to the retain data and augment it by a term promoting the orthogonality between the two gradients of the loss function evaluated at the retain dataset and the forget dataset. We coin this method unlearning via orthogonalization (UNO) and show that the additional weak orthogonality constraint accelerates unlearning. The inclusion of the weak orthogonality constraint implies that each gradient descent step utilizes local information about the geometry via the Hessian of the loss function. Our geometry aware gradient descent step significantly accelerates the learning of the retain data loss function compared to a gradient descent which uses only gradient information. By alternating between an UNO and a gradient surgery step, we obtain UNO-S, which further reduces execution time. We demonstrate that our algorithms effectively forget data while preserving the fidelity of the original model. On standard image benchmarks, they achieve orders-of-magnitude faster unlearning than existing methods such as gradient surgery. We validate our approach on datasets of increasing complexity (MNIST, CelebA, and ImageNet-1K) and generative architectures ranging from VAEs to diffusion transformers.

Machine Learning.title: Spacing Test for Fused Lasso
Machine Learning.summary: This paper studies the spacing test for the one-dimensional fused lasso. In post-selection inference for generalized lasso problems, the selective law is typically described by complicated polyhedral constraints, and the truncation limits of the resulting pivot are not available in simple closed form. We show that the one-dimensional fused lasso admits a remarkable simplification: the lower truncation boundary in the selective law coincides exactly with the next knot on the solution path. Consequently, the conservative spacing test of Tibshirani et al.~(2016), which is generally conservative in nonorthogonal settings, becomes exact for the one-dimensional fused lasso. The resulting selective $p$-value depends only on adjacent knots and has the same simple closed form as the ordinary LARS/lasso spacing statistic, without requiring additional polyhedral computations. Our analysis also gives a geometric interpretation of the fused-lasso path through a CUSUM representation of the knot values, connecting the spacing statistic with classical changepoint methods. Simulation studies confirm exact null calibration. Thus, the one-dimensional fused lasso provides a rare nontrivial example in the generalized-lasso family where exact post-selection inference is both theoretically explicit and computationally simple.

Machine Learning.title: Selective Data Expansion for Model Performance
Machine Learning.summary: Machine learning systems are increasingly being used in critical decision making such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice. Concerns around their fairness have resulted in several bias mitigation techniques that emphasize the need for high-quality data to ensure fairer decisions. However, the role of earlier stages of machine learning pipelines in mitigating model bias has not been explored well. In this paper, we focus on the task of acquiring additional labeled data points for training the downstream machine learning model to rapidly improve its fairness. Since not all data points in a data pool are equally beneficial to the task of fairness, we generate an ordering in which data points should be acquired. We present DataSift, a data acquisition framework based on the idea of data valuation that relies on partitioning and multi-armed bandits to determine the most valuable data points to acquire. Over several iterations, DataSift selects a partition and randomly samples a batch of data points from the selected partition, evaluates the benefit of acquiring the batch on model fairness, and updates the utility of partitions depending on the benefit. To further improve the effectiveness and efficiency of evaluating batches, we leverage influence functions that estimate the effect of acquiring a batch without retraining the model. We empirically evaluate DataSift on several real-world and synthetic datasets and show that the fairness of a machine learning model can be significantly improved even while acquiring a few data points.

Machine Learning.title: Causal inference and model explainability analysis of a real world sales dataset
Machine Learning.summary: Most major retailers today have multiple divisions focused on various aspects, such as marketing, supply chain, online customer experience, store customer experience, employee productivity, and vendor fulfillment. They also regularly collect data corresponding to all these aspects as dashboards and weekly/monthly/quarterly reports. Although several machine learning and statistical techniques have been in place to analyze and predict key metrics, such models typically lack interpretability. Moreover, such techniques also do not allow the validation or discovery of causal links. In this paper, we aim to provide a recipe for applying model interpretability and causal inference for deriving sales insights. In this paper, we review the existing literature on causal inference and interpretability in the context of problems in e-commerce and retail, and apply them to a real-world dataset. We find that an inherently explainable model has a lower variance of SHAP values, and show that including multiple confounders through a double machine learning approach allows us to get the correct sign of causal effect.

Machine Learning.title: Nexus : An Agentic Framework for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Language models have emerged as highly capable reasoners, yet their performance in time series forecasting remains uneven across domains and levels of contextual grounding. This is primarily due to their suboptimal time series reasoning and numerical modeling capabilities. To tackle this, we introduce Nexus, a multimodal forecasting framework that bridges qualitative event reasoning with structural numerical modeling through principled statistical synthesis. Nexus follows three structured stages: (1) Temporal profiling and anchor generation, which distills the multimodal history into a timestamped causal-temporal profile and generates a forecast anchor (2) Dual contextual outlook generation, which produces decoupled macro and micro level forecast trajectories, and (3) Bayesian synthesis, which reconciles the forecasting anchor with both contextual forecast trajectories via closed-form Gaussian updating weighted by empirical error covariances. Evaluated across three diverse forecasting benchmarks constituting eight datasets spanning rich event contexts, abrupt shocks, and purely numerical series, Nexus consistently outperforms leading time-series foundation models and language model baselines, while providing interpretable causal reasoning.

Machine Learning.title: Dynamic Neural Optimal Transport for Subset Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: We study optimal transport between distributions when only a subset of the target population is relevant to the source. The goal is to map the source distribution to a reweighted target distribution whose density ratio with respect to the full target lies in $[0, c]$. This constraint enables the transported distribution to select an appropriate target subpopulation while limiting how strongly any region of the target can be emphasized. We propose a dynamic neural optimal transport framework for this setting using two neural networks. The first parameterizes a time-dependent potential whose spatial gradient defines the velocity field and whose terminal value enforces the density-ratio constraint. The second parameterizes an interpolation between the source distribution and the learned terminal distribution. Unlike prior neural dynamic optimal transport methods, which typically assume a fixed terminal distribution, our formulation learns the terminal distribution within the support of the target. We demonstrate the method on positive-unlabeled learning, unpaired domain translation, and trajectory inference, where meaningful alignments exist between source and target distributions, but direct distribution matching is inappropriate because the target contains additional or irrelevant components

Machine Learning.title: Robustly Reliable Learning for Regression
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce the problem of robustly reliable learning for the regression setting in adversarial environments. Given a test point $x_{test}$, a training dataset $S$ of $n$ data points, a corruption budget $b \ll n$, and a real-valued hypothesis class $\mathcal H$, our goal is to output the optimal prediction range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$, such that any $L$-Lipschitz predictor consistent with all but at most $b$ points in $S$ must predict a value $h(x_{test}) \in I$. We then instantiate the analysis for $L$-Lipschitz hypothesis classes, a natural and widely studied class in the regression setting, focusing on two key scenarios. First, for the restricted case where the corrupted dataset is guaranteed to be $L$-Lipschitz consistent, we propose a simple and efficient $b^{th}$-best heuristic algorithm and prove its correctness in computing the tightest possible range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$. We then establish its computational complexity of $O(n)$ and show that it is computationally optimal in this scenario. Building on this foundation, we address the general scenario where the dataset $S$ is no longer $L$-Lipschitz consistent. We demonstrate that computing the optimal range in this setting reduces to analyzing a violation graph, which models the pairwise $L$-Lipschitz violations among data points. By leveraging the structural properties of this graph's kernel, we propose a Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) algorithm that computes the exact optimal range in $O(n^2 + b^4)$ time. Furthermore, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), we establish a computational lower bound of $Ω(n^{2 - o(1)})$, proving that our algorithm is computationally optimal. Finally, we discuss open directions for the problem of robustly reliable learning for regression.

Machine Learning.title: Cortex: A Fixed-Point Theory of Governed Coding Agents - Technical Report
Machine Learning.summary: A coding agent combines a large language model (LLM) with a harness that plans, edits, and executes code. We study Cortex, a supervisory layer for pre-execution governance, requirement tracking, and iterative validation and repair. We formalize requirement closure on a finite lattice. For a fixed requirement set and a sound, monotone validation rule with persistent evidence, exhaustive iteration reaches the least fixed point with no more strict increases than there are requirements. Fair consequence scheduling reaches the same closure. A separate stochastic model bounds expected completion time under a uniform positive-progress assumption. These results depend on their stated assumptions; artifact repair, fallible validation, and finite execution budgets do not satisfy them automatically. We define Gauntlet's trajectory-similarity and build-gated scores, attack-success estimators, Wilson intervals, and case-cluster bootstrap summaries. Effective-feedback accounting counts newly certified requirements, rather than estimating their information value or utility. The five evaluation families support raw-versus-governed comparisons. We report retained benchmark observations, including rescoring of existing artifacts; constructed outcomes are excluded. Unequal observation sets and incomplete provenance prevent causal claims about governance or measured long-horizon scaling.

Machine Learning.title: Can This LLM Annotate My Data? Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.

Machine Learning.title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning convex conformity scores that induce flexible, data-adaptive prediction regions. CoCoNet learns the score from held-out data by optimizing prediction-region efficiency while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}}$, based on piecewise-linear scores, and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{ICNN}}$, based on Input Convex Neural Networks. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. The results demonstrate the flexibility of CoCoNet in learning different response types. Across 8 models and 30 multi-dimensional regression tasks, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}\text{-}\ell_1}$ achieve the best efficiencies with average ranks of 1.45 and 2.75, respectively. In particular, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ ranks first on 22 tasks out of 30 in terms of efficiency.

Machine Learning.title: Optimal Post-Training Quantization Scales and Where to Find Them
Machine Learning.summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large language models by mapping weights to low-bit representations. While much work has focused on how weights are rounded onto the quantization grid, the scaling factor that defines the grid is typically chosen with simple, data-free heuristics. We observe that, under round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization, the grid assignments are piecewise constant in the scale, making the output reconstruction error piecewise quadratic over finitely many intervals, each admitting a closed-form optimization. Building on this insight, we present PiSO (Piecewise Scale Optimization), an algorithm that leverages calibration data to efficiently select channel-wise scales to achieve globally optimal output reconstruction error to arbitrary accuracy. We extend PiSO to group-wise quantization via tractable objectives. We also propose strategies for integrating it with error-correction methods such as GPTQ and Qronos, which greedily adjust weight assignments to compensate for the rounding errors of previously quantized weights. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models across multiple sizes and bit-widths show consistent improvements in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, both standalone and combined with error correction, with gains increasing as the bit-width narrows. For instance, on Llama-3, PiSO reduces the 2-bit perplexity of Qronos by up to 7x, and at 3 bits, PiSO without error correction outperforms GPTQ with absmax scales.
Machine Learning.comment: 9 pages excluding references and appendix, 39 pages total, 2 figures in the main text, 3 tables in the main text

Machine Learning.title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
Machine Learning.summary:
We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable.
  We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure.
  Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive.
  We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.

Machine Learning.title: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
Machine Learning.summary: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.

Machine Learning.title: EdgeRock: Strong Reasoning at Constant Memory
Machine Learning.summary: We present EdgeRock, a family of multimodal models that deliver strong reasoning at constant memory. Most models keep reasoning history in a key-value (KV) cache that grows with every token, consuming accelerator memory, limiting concurrent requests, and competing with perception and control on edge devices. With fixed history, memory is allocated once and never runs out, however long the model reasons. Constant memory alone is not new: bounded-state models (recurrent, state-space, and sliding-window) already achieve it, but often at the cost of reasoning, because they cannot keep the distant details that later reasoning needs. We therefore introduce Rock Memory Anchors (RMA): the model learns what is worth remembering and stores it as KV records in a fixed-size bank, directly readable however far back the source lies. EdgeRock-4B, our first open-source release, supports text and image reasoning and reaches 82.9% mean pass@1 on AIME 2024-2026, while the bounded-state models we evaluate reach at most 18.8%, even at 14B scale. This result is on par with leading compact models whose memory grows with reasoning. Compared with its source model, EdgeRock-4B uses up to 99.1% less KV cache and delivers up to 6.42$\times$ higher end-to-end batch throughput.
Machine Learning.comment: 24 pages, 8 figures. Substantially revised technical report under the EdgeRock name, with expanded evaluation and deployment results. Code: https://github.com/rockmatrix-ai/EdgeRock ; Model: https://huggingface.co/rockmatrix-ai/EdgeRock

Machine Learning.title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it.
