When stylization modifies this combined colour, the illumination effects present during stylization are baked into the stored appearance, so the stylized scene cannot be rendered under different illumination. To address this limitation, we present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware 3D Gaussian representation. Rather than modifying a per-point RGB colour, RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field recovered by inverse rendering, while leaving roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and the estimated environment lighting unchanged. As a result, the stylized scene keeps all the components a physically-based renderer needs other than the edited albedo, and can therefore still be relit. RxGS optimizes the albedo field using a nearest-neighbour feature matching loss together with a spatial smoothness prior over Gaussian centres. We evaluate the method using a Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) based on optical-flow warping error. RxGS achieves the lowest GCC on all evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scenes and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while additionally supporting relightable stylization, which existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods do not provide.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Frechet Forcing: Training Long-Horizon Streaming World Models from Short Clips
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Streaming video world models generate the future chunk by chunk, conditioned on their own past and a stream of actions. Trained on short clips, they drift once a rollout exceeds the training horizon, as prediction errors re-enter the context and compound. A common remedy is to train the model on its own rollouts via distribution matching distillation (DMD). For action-conditioned world models, the teacher becomes a bottleneck: an external video model is agnostic to the actions, whereas the model's own pretrained network drifts in the same manner as the student. We observe that a long rollout need not match a teacher, provided it remains a realistic continuation of its own scene that follows the commanded actions. Realism and scene fidelity can be measured against real-data statistics, which remain valid at any horizon, while action following is preserved by the model's conditional generation loss. We propose Fréchet Forcing, which fine-tunes a world model together with its deployed multi-step sampler under three constraints. Generative anchoring applies the flow-matching loss after a self-generated history ending on real data. Context fidelity, a Fréchet distance (FD) on latent statistics of the free rollout centred on each clip's own ground truth, keeps every rollout faithful to its scene. Reality matching, an FD to real frames in a frozen perceptual space, keeps the generated frames realistic. Because all three targets are derived from short real clips without comparing a rollout against a long recorded future, training requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos. Fine-tuning MiniWorld-1B, pretrained on 253-frame clips, for at most 36 GPU-hours on 381-frame clips yields rollouts that remain stable beyond 4,000 frames and continue to follow their actions in both robot manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SpaRV: Sparse Radiance Voxels for Scalable Geometrically Consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Robotic simulation, navigation, and inspection need photorealistic and geometrically accurate maps. Radiance fields achieve photorealism, but building them from robot data raises three challenges. A robot's trajectory serves its task, not reconstruction, so images from few viewpoints leave the geometry under-constrained. Residual errors in camera poses and intrinsics blur the map. The map's GPU memory grows with scene size, which limits its level of detail in large scenes. We present \textbf{SpaRV}, a \textbf{Spa}rse \textbf{R}adiance \textbf{V}oxel map rendered by differentiable ray marching, which lets irregular LiDAR scans supervise it alongside images. LiDAR depth and occupancy anchor the under-constrained geometry, and normal and smoothness regularizers keep it smooth between LiDAR points. To correct camera errors, SpaRV alternates map training with photometric optimization of the camera poses and focal lengths. To bound GPU memory in training and rendering, SpaRV holds one submap at a time at full resolution and the rest at coarser octree levels. Experiments show that SpaRV keeps the geometry consistent away from the captured trajectory and sharpens textures by optimizing the camera parameters. On one 24\,GB GPU, SpaRV reconstructs a university campus captured in 63{,}582 images and simulates other cameras and LiDARs. Our code will be released at \url{https://github.com/hku-mars/SpaRV}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose \textbf{PoSTCache} (\emph{Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache}), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality--efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Post-Training Frontier Text-to-Image Models by Composing Preference and Rubric Rewards
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent text-to-image generation models have achieved remarkable visual quality, but improving them through post-training remains challenging because no single reward signal captures the full range of human preference. In this work, we develop a simple and effective post-training recipe for open-domain text-to-image generation based on the composition of complementary reward signals. Our reward system consists of two main components: a preference reward, trained on large-scale human preference data using a Bradley-Terry objective to capture overall human aesthetic and perceptual preferences, and rubric-based rewards, which explicitly evaluate prompt faithfulness and other desirable properties while providing safeguards against reward hacking. A key challenge is how to combine these heterogeneous reward signals. We show that a naive weighted average leads to suboptimal optimization behavior, and propose a simple reward composition strategy that more effectively balances preference optimization with rubric satisfaction. In the Arena text-to-image leaderboard (https://arena.ai/), our RL-trained Flux2dev achieves an Elo rating 69 points above the base model, and our post-trained Ideogram-4 surpasses every open-source model on the leaderboard, reaching an Elo of 1223.5. (Claims of state-of-the-art performance are based on the Arena leaderboard snapshot as of September 4, 2026.) Our results suggest that effective rewards for frontier generative-model training require broad coverage of user intent and robustness to exploitation under optimization. To support reproducible research, we release Arena-T2I-Training, a 1K subset of training data that recovers some gains of full-scale training, providing a resource that we hope will facilitate future work on post-training for text-to-image models.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LUMIN: Lifecycle-Utility-aware and Metadata-Informed Network for Visual Anomaly Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Industrial anomaly detection faces two engineering bottlenecks: memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency. Traditional sampling algorithms (Farthest Point Sampling, K-Means, etc.) rely on numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, with construction times ranging from minutes to hours; heavy computation components such as multi-scale feature extraction struggle to meet the millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines. This paper focuses on sampling efficiency and inference optimization for industrial deployment with two core contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline)---a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline based on 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins. PSP completes all sampling with zero backbone forward passes; coarse filtering is sub-second numerical sorting, and metadata extraction is a one-time offline cost. PSP supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies---parallel memory bank similarity computation (reducing inference memory and latency by over 95\%) and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (reducing computation time by 20$\times$ while keeping metrics stable). As a vehicle for validation, we introduce LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression, systematically exploring the accuracy-efficiency frontier against strong baselines. Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost (341$\times$ faster than FPS), while inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20$\times$ with negligible accuracy loss.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: InteractAgent: Agentic Human Motion Interaction with Memory-Augmented Reflection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-horizon human-scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text-driven motion models are largely scene-agnostic and lack closed-loop correction, while geometry-conditioned approaches depend on paired scene-motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open-vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long-horizon human-scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step-wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory-Augmented Reflection for multi-round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training-free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SatFix: Absolute Visual Localization of UAVs in Satellite Maps from a Single Oblique Image
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We study absolute metric UAV localization within a provided geo-referenced satellite region, recovering continuous map position and viewing heading from a single oblique image or a short multi-view clip. Existing cross-view geo-localization methods retrieve the most similar satellite tile from a gallery and report Recall@K, but retrieval depends on gallery sampling, provides no heading estimate, and returns a tile index rather than a continuous coordinate. We propose SatFix, a feed-forward UAV--satellite localization framework built on VGGT-$Ω$. Satellite-grid features act as queries that aggregate UAV visual evidence, and two lightweight heads regress a 3-DoF pose in the satellite-map frame: continuous 2D position and heading. SatFix requires no explicit 3D map, rendered bird's-eye image, auxiliary sensor, or test-time pose alignment. A single model supports both single- and multi-view inputs, with trajectory constraints used during multi-view training. For metric evaluation, we introduce University-Metric, where satellite imagery is re-collected over a region up to 10.7$\times$ longer on a side (about 114$\times$ the ground area) than the original University-1652 tiles, with continuous position and heading labels for the original UAV tours. With one UAV view, SatFix localizes 52.08% of test frames within 50 m and 17.34% within 10 m, with median position and heading errors of 45.66 m and $20.81^\circ$, respectively. Inference takes under 0.1 s per single-view query on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. With nine UAV views, the median position error falls to 21.96 m and the median heading error to $8.73^\circ$. Compared with a fine-tuned VGGT-$Ω$ baseline, SatFix reduces median position error by 34.0% and nine-view median heading error from $25.43^\circ$ to $8.73^\circ$.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Satellite images at multiple resolutions are available at: https://1drv.ms/u/c/758af5fc520c81c5/IQCjvHc3iiq6SJDpYipcIv5vAc-NmHMPCAwSTBnrA1vhM5U?e=YSX1lZ UAV images can be downloaded from the original University-1652 dataset

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Negation without Confusion: Decomposing Bias and Recomposing Style in Text Embeddings for Negation-aware Image Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Negation-aware image generation remains challenging for text-to-image diffusion models, which often struggle with negation due to implicit linguistic biases that are deeply entangled within text representations. As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of Decompose and Recompose text embedding (Dero), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, Dero realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, Dero can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Visual Memory and Textual Alignment for Cross-Modal Few-Shot Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Few-shot segmentation (FSS) aims to segment target objects with limited annotated examples. Recent studies have begun to explore large foundation models to improve generalization for this task. In particular, SAM 3 provides strong visual representations and supports text-guided segmentation. However, its performance remains limited in specialized domains, where semantic prompts and visual representations are often poorly aligned. To address this challenge, we propose ViTA-SAM, a framework built upon SAM 3 that integrates visual memory and textual features through cross-modal alignment. Specifically, we construct a visual memory module that encodes support features together with their corresponding masks, providing support-aware visual guidance for query prediction. In parallel, we leverage the text encoder of SAM 3 to extract semantic features as complementary priors. To bridge the gap between semantic and visual representations, we introduce a cross-modal alignment module that conditions textual features on memory-enhanced visual representations, yielding more consistent and visually grounded predictions. In addition, we propose a pseudo-label refinement strategy that updates the memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive representation learning. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ViTA-SAM achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods, outperforming the strongest competing method by over 5% in average mIoU.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TNVD-SC: Diagnosing Scan Context Failures in Forests with Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distributions
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-term LiDAR place recognition in forests is difficult because repetitive vegetation and uneven terrain create severe structural aliasing. We diagnose Scan Context (SC) by separating candidate retrieval from fine matching: on the standardized TreeLoc++ Wild-Places protocol, a TNVD support key places a valid location in the top-25 set for approximately 99% of queries, while conventional SC matching on those candidates reaches only 61.84% mean R@1. With an identical raw-SC candidate set, terrain normalization improves max-height cells by only 1.21 points but vertical-distribution cells by 19.72 points. These observations motivate Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distribution Scan Context (TNVD-SC), which preserves the SC ring-sector topology while encoding terrain-relative vertical probability distributions. Under the standardized TreeLoc++ protocol, TNVD-SC reaches 91.83% mean R@1 and attains the highest R@1 mean and R@1 stability among the compared methods, while TreeLoc++ remains stronger in mean MR, MF1, and AUC. The unchanged method reaches 85.14% mean R@1 on the four-session CVTNet-style NCLT evaluation. A lossless count-coded implementation with exact hierarchical Jensen-Shannon search reduces descriptor payload by 3.86x and compute latency by 23.8% without changing the audited retrieval outputs.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Confidence-Guided Pseudo-Label Refinement for Unsupervised Cross-Domain Person Re-Identification
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Unsupervised cross-domain person re-identification remains challenging because domain shifts generate noisy pseudo labels that are reinforced during iterative adaptation. Existing clustering-based methods often rely on limited reliability cues or global confidence criteria and may impose hard identity supervision on ambiguous target samples. To address these limitations, we propose CGPLR, a confidence-guided pseudo-label refinement framework for unsupervised domain-adaptive person re-identification. CGPLR estimates sample-level reliability by jointly modeling centroid compatibility, local neighborhood consistency, separation from the strongest competing cluster and temporal assignment stability. The resulting confidence distribution is used to derive cluster-adaptive upper and lower thresholds for a three-way selective decision. Reliable assignments are preserved, recoverable samples are reassigned only when an alternative cluster receives sufficient geometric and neighborhood support and highly ambiguous samples are deferred from hard identity supervision. The learning objective adapts to these decisions through confidence-weighted supervision for preserved samples, cautious corrected-label weighting for reassigned samples and label-free representation consistency for deferred samples. CGPLR achieves 76.4% Rank-1 accuracy and 47.6% mean average precision (mAP) on Market-1501 to MSMT17, and 95.1% Rank-1 accuracy and 87.7% mAP on MSMT17 to Market-1501, demonstrating effective reliability-aware selective adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/Sundas058/CGPLR.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SIGMA: Semantic-Difference Instruction-Grounding Mask Annotator for Text-Driven Image Manipulation Localization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Text-driven image editing has advanced rapidly, but reliably localizing these manipulations requires image manipulation localization (IML) models trained on large pixel-annotated datasets, and there is still no low-cost way to obtain such training data at scale. We observe that these data already exist in disguise: public editing datasets contain millions of structurally identical $\textit{(original, edited)}$ pairs to IML training samples, lacking only pixel-level masks. Recovering these masks automatically is non-trivial: pixel differencing is overwhelmed by diffusion-induced perturbations across all pixels, and instruction-only grounding localizes only what the prompt describes, missing unintended editor side-effects. We propose $\textbf{SIGMA}$ ($\textbf{S}$emantic-difference $\textbf{I}$nstruction-$\textbf{G}$rounding $\textbf{M}$ask $\textbf{A}$nnotator), which performs semantic-feature differencing in a vision foundation backbone and injects an instruction-derived spatial prior into this visual stream via bidirectional cross-modal refinement, amplifying the difference signal at intended-edit regions when the editor faithfully realizes user intent. SIGMA is trained in two complementary stages: Stage I supervises on inpainting masks and Stage II closes the diffusion-domain shift via VAE-roundtrip noise calibration, EMA self-training, and an edit-noise disentanglement loss. SIGMA outperforms existing automatic mask generators on five benchmarks ($\textbf{+12.20\%}$ F1, $\textbf{+11.16\%}$ IoU). When applied to public editing corpora, it produces a $\sim$1.1M IML training set that improves four diverse detectors by $\textbf{+20.98\%}$ F1 across five datasets, turning previously unused editing data into a model-agnostic supervisory resource for IML. For reproducibility, our project page is available at \url{https://zhuangpeiyu.github.io/projects/SIGMA/}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Where Do the Gaussians Go? Foreground Attraction for Camera-Based Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy models can be trained without 3D labels by rendering their predictions into the images and supervising them with 2D pseudo labels. In sparse Gaussian representations trained this way, Gaussian positions are learned only through pixel-wise rendering losses, which we hypothesize give small foreground objects little weight. In trained GaussianFlowOcc models, the Gaussian density on foreground voxels is on average only 1.62 times that on background voxels. We propose a training-only foreground attraction loss that back-projects foreground pseudo-label pixels with pseudo depth and pulls nearby Gaussians toward these 3D points, favoring Gaussians that already predict the target class; the inference network is unchanged. On Occ3D-nuScenes, the loss raises this concentration to 2.40 over three seeds. Over three seeds, the mean foreground IoU increases from 6.29 to 6.96 and is higher for each seed, whereas the change in mean mIoU (13.53 to 13.82) is within the seed-to-seed variation of the baseline. Single-run ablations further indicate that pseudo-label targets outperform targets placed at ground-truth voxels and that acting on the Gaussian positions alone is not sufficient, and a single-seed test shows that the model degrades less when fewer Gaussians are kept at inference.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: From Scientific Crop Imagery to Agronomic Reasoning: A Multimodal LLM Benchmark for Plant Phenotyping
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: High-throughput, effective and comprehensive phenotyping is a critical prerequisite for crop improvement. While phenotypic analysis was traditionally performed manually, recent advances in multimodal foundation models, especially in vision-language models, have offered new opportunities for automated plant phenotyping. However, plant science remains particularly challenging for general-purpose VLMs because it requires domain-specific knowledge, fine-grained visual interpretation, and complex agronomic reasoning. We introduce PlantXpert, an evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning benchmark for plant phenotyping across four major crops: soybean, cotton, rice, and corn. Our benchmark provides a structured and reproducible framework for agronomic adaptation of VLMs, and enables controlled comparison between base models and their domain-adapted counterparts. We constructed a dataset comprising 545 digital images and 4,351 benchmark samples spanning key agronomic domains including disease, pest control, weed management and yield. The benchmark can assess diverse capabilities including visual expertise, quantitative reasoning, and multi-step agronomic reasoning. We trained and evaluated a total of 11 state-of-the-art VLMs. Fine-tuning on our dataset improves overall accuracy for all models, with many achieving around 70% accuracy, and improvements on 9 of 11 remaining statistically significant after Holm correction. We also identify diminishing returns from model scaling, uneven performance across crop subsets, and persistent weaknesses in quantitative reasoning and specialized image analysis. These limitations show that general multimodal competence alone is insufficient for reliable agronomic reasoning and demonstrate the value of domain-specific adaptation. We hope PlantXpert can serve as a foundation for advancing evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in plant science.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Recurrent Vision Transformers for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation Under Slow Relative Motions
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-based object pose estimation is vital for conducting spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO). Recent research has demonstrated the robustness of event cameras against the harsh lighting conditions that often occur in orbit, thanks to the extremely high dynamic range of event sensors. However, event-based spacecraft pose estimation (EBSPE) suffers when the relative motion between the chaser and target is slow, since the event rate drops significantly, leading to data with low signal-to-noise ratio. Unfortunately, for safety reasons, real RPO trajectories often involve slow relative motions (e.g., down to 1 mm/s), and operating under low illumination exacerbates the problem. Addressing slow relative motions is thus crucial to raise the practicality of EBSPE. To this end, we propose using recurrent vision transformers (RVT) for EBSPE. The key idea is to exploit recurrent memory to capture longer-term information across sparse event streams, and to learn the temporal attention span from full trajectories rather than fixing the time window. We developed an RVT-based heatmap regressor to produce 2D-3D correspondences for pose estimation, which was validated on real event data collected under slow relative motions representative of RPO trajectories. Results indicate the superior pose estimation accuracy and stability of our RVT-based method, relative to previous per-event-frame-based or fixed-time-window EBSPE methods.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Virtual Encoders in Multimodal Transformers
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal language models traditionally rely on dedicated perceptual encoders to construct task-usable representations. More integrated architectures have recently emerged, which instead expose the shared transformer to lightly projected patches, audio frames, or discrete visual tokens. Where does this encoding happen when such representations are not provided? We find that the transformer can internalize this missing computation, constructing task-usable perceptual representations within its own early-to-middle layers before the downstream language model. We call this computational structure a Virtual Encoder. Across linear probing, similarities to perceptual encoders, and causal analyses, we identify signatures of this structure in models that receive perceptual tokens without continuous encoder-derived features. These analyses also suggest that the boundary between perception and language processing need not coincide within an architectural module. Instead, encoder-like computation can emerge as a functional regime within a shared transformer, providing a new perspective for understanding where and how multimodal models process perception.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at ACCV 2026 Workshop on Subspaces

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Why VLMs Miss Small Objects, and When Zooming In Is Safe
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often miss small objects in large images. We ask three questions: what limits them, which of these limits better models can remove, and whether the classical way of handling large images, local decomposition, still has a future. We answer them with a theory built on two quantities of the image interface: S, the number of visual tokens across an object's side, and L, the content a call must cover. The limits: a W x H image sent whole within N tokens gives an object of side m at most m*sqrt(N/(WH)) tokens per side. Doubling the token budget N therefore raises the largest S a whole image can reach by only 41%, and seeing an image at the S an object needs costs at least order S^2 tokens whatever the model. If recognition improves gradually with S, any search strategy, zoom agents included, obeys a recall-cost frontier. What better models can change: the S an object needs and how much one call can carry, measured in bits per object found; the coverage cost remains. Decomposition: yes. Assuming only that more tokens per object and less content per call do not hurt on average, splitting an image cannot lower expected recall if no view zooms out relative to the whole image and views overlap by one object. Neither part can be dropped; we bound the cost of every such decomposition, and a simple rule approaches the bound as the image grows. We test the theory in about 177,000 requests on 797 images. On controlled images, none of 40 orderings predicted for 8 VLMs is violated. Checked after the fact on drawings, floor plans, natural and synthetic images, 61 of 89 implied orderings hold significantly and 4 fail, all for OpenAI models given more pixels than their default path. On construction drawings the rule never significantly lowered recall relative to the whole image and raised it by up to 0.28. Code and data: https://github.com/shijunzhe/vlm-small-objects

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CMFDFormer: Transformer-based Copy-Move Forgery Detection with Continual Learning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Copy-move forgery detection aims at detecting duplicated regions in a suspected forged image, and deep learning based copy-move forgery detection methods are in the ascendant. These deep learning based methods heavily rely on synthetic training data, and the performance will degrade when facing new tasks. In this paper, we propose a Transformer-style copy-move forgery detection network named as CMFDFormer, and provide a novel PCSD (Pooled Cube and Strip Distillation) continual learning framework to help CMFDFormer handle new tasks. CMFDFormer consists of a MiT (Mix Transformer) backbone network and a PHD (Pluggable Hybrid Decoder) mask prediction network. The MiT backbone network is a Transformer-style network which is adopted on the basis of comprehensive analyses with CNN-style and MLP-style backbones. The PHD network is constructed based on self-correlation computation, hierarchical feature integration, a multi-scale cycle fully-connected block and a mask reconstruction block. The PHD network is applicable to feature extractors of different styles for hierarchical multi-scale information extraction, achieving comparable performance. Last but not least, we propose a PCSD continual learning framework to improve the forgery detectability and avoid catastrophic forgetting when handling new tasks. Our continual learning framework restricts intermediate features from the PHD network, and takes advantage of both cube pooling and strip pooling. Extensive experiments on publicly available datasets demonstrate the good performance of CMFDFormer and the effectiveness of the PCSD continual learning framework.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: The method has been further improved and additional experiments have been added. As the revised version differs substantially from this version, this version is therefore withdrawn.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Retargeting Motions to Diverse Skeletons via Learnable Flattening
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Cross-structural motion retargeting aims to transfer motion between different skeletal topologies. Despite recent progress, existing state-of-the-art models struggle with reliability in zero-shot settings, i.e. skeletons with different topologies which were unseen during training, and recent Transformer-based attempts have failed to outperform specialized geometric methods. We bridge this gap with a Transformer Autoencoder that learns a topology- and translation-invariant latent space. Our core contribution is a learnable flattening of skeletal graphs that captures both local dependencies and global structure. Unlike the standard transformer architecture, which adds positional information to token content, we integrate graph-based positional encodings multiplicatively, a design choice that follows directly from our flattening formulation. The resulting model handles diverse skeletal topologies within a single unified architecture and trains in a fully unsupervised manner, requiring no paired retargeting data. Ablation studies show, that the graph encodings, multiplicative formulation, and Transformer backbone is critical for the performance. In zero-shot evaluations, our method reduces global joint position error by $43-47\%$ over current benchmarks. A user study ($n = 37$), including expert animators, further ranks our approach highest in motion alignment and physical plausibility ($p < 0.05$). These results demonstrate that our model design is key to making transformer architectures effective for motion retargeting, outperforming existing approaches.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PALATE: Peculiar Application of the Law of Total Expectation to Enhance the Evaluation of Deep Generative Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Deep generative models (DGMs) have caused a paradigm shift in the field of machine learning, yielding noteworthy advancements in domains such as image synthesis, natural language processing, and other related areas. However, a comprehensive evaluation of these models that effectively captures the interplay among fidelity, diversity, and novelty in generated samples remains a persistent challenge. A recently proposed approach, the Feature Likelihood Divergence (FLD), offers a theoretically grounded and practical tool in this regard but faces notable computational limitations. In this paper, we propose PALATE, a novel framework designed to enhance the evaluation of DGMs by addressing the efficiency constraints of FLD. Our approach is based on a peculiar application of the law of total expectation to random variables representing accessible data. When integrated with the MMD baseline metric and the recently introduced DINOv3 feature extractor, PALATE provides a comprehensive evaluation framework that matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods while offering superior computational efficiency and scalability to large-scale datasets. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that the PALATE enhancement constitutes a practical and computationally efficient framework for holistic DGM assessment, particularly in detecting sample memorization and evaluating generalization capabilities. The source code is provided as supplementary material.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Neural image codecs face a fundamental trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality. Distortion-optimized codecs preserve pixel-wise fidelity but produce blurred reconstructions at low bitrates, whereas generative codecs leverage learned priors to improve perceptual quality but tend to exhibit saturating PSNR at higher bitrates and require separate models for different bitrate targets. We propose PerQ, which reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we define the quantization cell as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols and derive a transport bound showing that reconstructions from this cell remain within a rate-determined radius of the codec output. This motivates performing generative reconstruction within the codec-induced quantization cell, rather than sampling from an unconstrained image prior. PerQ implements this principle by attaching a rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator to a frozen, multi-rate distortion-optimized backbone, enabling perceptual enhancement while preserving the backbone's coding performance. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 show that PerQ achieves perceptual performance comparable to generative codecs such as MS-ILLM in LPIPS and FID, while maintaining competitive PSNR relative to distortion-optimized codecs such as ELIC. A single model checkpoint supports a wide bitrate range with fast decoding, and the compensator provides consistent gains across three different backbones. The implementation is available at https://jasminepp.github.io/PerQ/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Look Before You Reason: Implicit Visual Thinking for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. We first show that this contextually appropriate granularity is recoverable from pre-generation hidden states, even when generated responses are misaligned, with disclosure levels exhibiting an ordered structure along a common hidden-state direction. Motivated by this, we propose an inference-time route-and-steer framework: an ordinal granularity router maps visual-contextual privacy representations to a disclosure route, and a disclosure-level-conditioned steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. Across four VLM backbones, our method improves visual-context-aware disclosure alignment, better balances over- and under-disclosure, and incurs only modest changes on general capability benchmarks. It further transfers to another dataset with a distinct data distribution and privacy-risk taxonomy.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: What Not to Erase: Saliency-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource Handwritten Character Recognition
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and handwritten character recognition (HCR) in low-resource historical material collections often rely on data augmentation, yet augmentation strategies are typically evaluated almost exclusively through predictive accuracy. This leaves open whether a model's improved performance is accompanied by saliency stability. This question is important in low-resource historical HCR, where recognition is performed on variable and partially degraded letterforms and two models with similar predictive performance may differ in how consistently their saliency patterns respond to such variation. We therefore study saliency-guided augmentation as an explanation-aware strategy for low-resource HCR. Rather than treating saliency maps only as post-hoc interpretations, we use them to define augmentation variants that perturb, preserve, or constrain visually informative regions of character images. We compare classical document-style transformations, random lacunae, and several saliency-constrained lacuna variants. To evaluate the effect of augmentation beyond accuracy, we introduce the Explainability Consistency Index (ECI), a metric that quantifies the stability of saliency patterns under controlled perturbations. We find that saliency-constrained augmentation can improve recognition over classical augmentation, but no single saliency strategy is consistently best. The preferred form of the constraint varies with both architecture and corpus, indicating that saliency is better treated as a mechanism for controlling augmentation than as a fixed augmentation strategy. In some settings, saliency-constrained training improves explanation consistency even when predictive performance is similar. This shows that predictive metrics alone can obscure differences in model sensitivity under perturbation, motivating explanation consistency as a complementary evaluation dimension.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LADDER: Landmark-Only Lip-Sync Deepfake Detection Across Generators and Languages
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We propose LADDER, a lip-sync deepfake detector that uses only the trajectories of 64 lip landmarks. It needs no pixels and no audio. We find two problems that make such a detector fail across domains. First, frame rate is a confounding factor. On PolyGlotFake, real and fake videos differ in frame rate, and the direction of this difference changes across languages. We remove it by resampling every trajectory to 25 fps. Second, motion amplitude does not transfer across generators: some generators move the mouth more than real speakers, and others move it less. The slope across derivative orders does transfer, because it is higher in fake videos for all five generators we test. LADDER combines a small trained detector (0.31 M parameters) with a prior score that needs no training: the mean of the slope features, standardized on real videos only. Learning this direction from data, or selecting it on the training domain, transfers worse. LADDER runs at 7.2 times real time on one CPU core. It reaches 0.925 AUC on LipSyncTIMIT at CRF=23 and 0.850 on seven languages of PolyGlotFake, comparable to pixel-based and audio-visual detectors. It is also more robust than a retrained Xception and is ahead in all 14 settings with stronger compression or image corruption, for example 0.883 against 0.579 under strong blur. Finally, a decision threshold does not transfer across domains, but 20 unlabeled real videos bring the false positive rate back to at most 3.5%.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Keywords: Deepfake detection, lip-sync, facial landmarks, domain generalization, frame rate, cross-lingual, robustness

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RoboFake: Are Deepfake Detectors Ready for Humanoid Face Robots?
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Humanoid face robots can now move their lips in sync with speech and show detailed facial expressions. Give such a robot the face of a real person and drive it with generated speech, and you get a new kind of presentation attack: a face that talks and reacts in front of the camera, recorded as a real object with no edited pixel. We call this a RoboFake and ask whether current defenses are ready for it. We test three public face presentation attack detection (PAD) models and six public deepfake detectors on video of a physical lip-syncing face robot, on a synthesized video of the same robot, and on rendered robot faces. Thresholds are fixed on human data (BPCER 5% on FaceForensics++), and every result is compared with real human faces processed the same way as the robot videos and turned to the same head angle. A small mobile PAD model detects every physical robot frame (APCER 0%) and is not affected by compression, but its BPCER on processed human video rises to 14%; the two PAD models trained on CelebA-Spoof miss the robot in the direct capture, and one of them also misses most panel frames. Among the deepfake detectors, three flag almost every robot frame and two fewer than 7%; masking shows that the response comes from the face but does not track synthesis, and JPEG compression pushes most robot frames below the threshold for some detectors. Our results suggest that current models catch today's robots because their faces do not look human, not because they recognize the attack. We state three testable hypotheses about realistic, interactive RoboFakes.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Keywords: Deepfake detection, presentation attack detection, face anti-spoofing, humanoid robots, face robots, biometric security, robustness

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: This work has been accepted in WACV 2027

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ReRef-3D: A Benchmark for Spatial Referring Expression-Guided 3D Object Placement
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce ReRef-3D, a benchmark for language-guided single-object placement in controlled 3D tabletop scenes. It contains 33,826 instructions across 998 CLEVR-derived scenes, spanning 16 placement types and direct, one-hop, and two-hop references. Given that an instruction defines a region of acceptable placements rather than one coordinate, predictions are evaluated by relation satisfaction and physical validity. Each instruction also includes a verified natural rephrasing. We evaluate LLaVA-3D, 3D-LLM, 3D-LLaVA, LL3DA, and PlaceIt3D, with PlaceIt3D evaluated under both point-based and region-based supervision. Region-supervised PlaceIt3D achieves the highest placement accuracy at about 80% and LLaVA-3D reaches about 70%. Performance varies by relation type, but nearest and aligned remain the most difficult. Rephrasing has little effect on performance overall.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 18 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to ACL Rolling Review (ARR)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CARI4D: Category Agnostic 4D Reconstruction of Human-Object Interaction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Accurate capture of human-object interaction from ubiquitous sensors like RGB cameras is important for applications in human understanding, gaming, and robot learning. However, inferring 4D interactions from a single RGB view is highly challenging due to the unknown object and human information, depth ambiguity, occlusion, and complex motion, which hinder consistent 3D and temporal reconstruction. Previous methods simplify the setup by assuming ground truth object template or constraining to a limited set of object categories. We present CARI4D, the first category-agnostic method that reconstructs spatially and temporarily consistent 4D human-object interaction at metric scale from monocular RGB videos. To this end, we propose a pose hypothesis selection algorithm that robustly integrates the individual predictions from foundation models, jointly refine them through a learned render-and-compare paradigm to ensure spatial, temporal and pixel alignment, and finally reasoning about intricate contacts for further refinement satisfying physical constraints. Experiments show that our method outperforms prior art by 38% on in-distribution dataset and 36% on unseen dataset in terms of reconstruction error. Our model generalizes beyond the training categories and thus can be applied zero-shot to in-the-wild internet videos. Our code and pretrained models will be publicly released.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Update table 1 and table 2 after fixing a bug in evaluation

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration in robotics. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests. Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood. We study this relationship theoretically. We show that a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than the maximum consensus set at any fixed positive tolerance, and derive geometric conditions that bound this error. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem. Finally, we study group-$k$ consistency, which tests groups of $k$ matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are $d+1$ for rotations and translations and $d+2$ when reflections are allowed, in dimensions $d\ge 2$. Interactive examples and proof verification using the Lean theorem prover are available at https://ariarobotics.github.io/mc-vs-mc-registration/.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Interactive examples and Lean proof verification: https://ariarobotics.github.io/mc-vs-mc-registration/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TokenSwap: Benchmarking and Reducing the Modality Gap in Multimodal LLMs
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should exhibit cross-modal consistency, generating consistent responses given semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. However, we observe a systematic discrepancy in model predictions under such cross-modal variations. Specifically, we define the modality gap as the difference in model performance under semantically equivalent textual and multimodal inputs. We introduce TokenSwap, a method that constructs such inputs by replacing textual concepts with semantically aligned images, resulting in sequences where visual tokens are interleaved with text tokens. Based on TokenSwap, we transform existing text-based benchmarks (e.g., MMLU) into image-interleaved counterparts, resulting in TokenSwap-Bench. Across 42 MLLMs, we observe a pervasive modality gap, with performance decreasing by 4.2% to 47.4% when moving from text-only to image-interleaved inputs, averaging 19.6% +/- 3.3% across models. Notably, reasoning models exhibit consistently smaller gaps, achieving an average gap of 10.1% compared to 25.5% for non-reasoning models, suggesting greater robustness in multimodal reasoning across equivalent textual and visual representations. In contrast, neither prompting strategies nor scaling training compute alone reliably reduces the modality gap. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating TokenSwap during training effectively mitigates this gap, improving cross-modal alignment while preserving strong text-only and vision-language model performance. The project page is available at https://dongxzz.github.io/TokenSwap/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Where to Look Matters: Rethinking Sub-Volume Sampling in 3D Medical Self-supervised Learning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Self-supervised learning on 3D medical images commonly relies on random sub-volume sampling during pretraining. However, random cropping implicitly treats all spatial regions as equally worth observing, despite anatomical priors and spatial redundancy that make regions inherently unequal in their value for representation learning. To this end, we first show through controlled crop-quality manipulations that better sub-volumes lead to better downstream transfer, revealing the observation policy as an overlooked bottleneck in 3D medical SSL. Motivated by this finding, we revisit sub-volume sampling as a where-to-look problem. We propose VolumeProbe, a plug-and-play framework that replaces random cropping with an offline coarse-to-fine probe bank guided by anatomy-awareness, informativeness, and diversity. We instantiate VolumeProbe as a lightweight Lite variant using geometric and image-statistical cues, and a diagnostic Feat variant using frozen visual features, to examine whether lightweight volume-intrinsic priors suffice or richer semantic cues reliably provide additional value. Extensive experiments across multiple 3D medical SSL backbones and downstream tasks demonstrate that VolumeProbe-Lite consistently improves transfer performance over random sampling. Mechanistic analyses further link these gains to more anatomically plausible and informative observations, reduced spatial redundancy, more efficient learning dynamics, and more structured representations.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TrajTok: Learning Trajectory Tokens enables better Video Understanding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Tokenization in video models, typically through patchification, generates an excessive and redundant number of tokens. This severely limits video efficiency and scalability. While recent trajectory-based tokenizers offer a promising solution by decoupling video duration from token count, they rely on complex external segmentation and tracking pipelines that are slow and task-agnostic. We propose TrajTok, an end-to-end video tokenizer module that is fully integrated and co-trained with video models for a downstream objective, dynamically adapting its token granularity to semantic complexity, independent of video duration. TrajTok contains a unified segmenter that performs implicit clustering over pixels in both space and time to directly produce object trajectories in a single forward pass. By prioritizing downstream adaptability over pixel-perfect segmentation fidelity, TrajTok is lightweight and efficient, yet empirically improves video understanding performance. With TrajTok, we implement a video CLIP model trained from scratch (TrajViT2). It achieves the best accuracy at scale across both classification and retrieval benchmarks, while maintaining efficiency comparable to the best token-merging methods. TrajTok also proves to be a versatile component beyond its role as a tokenizer. We show that it can be seamlessly integrated as either a probing head for pretrained visual features (TrajAdapter) or an alignment connector in vision-language models (TrajVLM) with especially strong performance in long-video reasoning.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Language Guidance for Supervised Vision Training: An Empirical Study of Generalization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success on vision benchmarks, yet they continue to struggle with many generalization challenges. Supervised vision training relies on one-hot labels, which provide limited information about semantic structure and shared attributes between classes. This limited supervision can leave visual representations vulnerable to distribution shifts, spurious correlations, texture bias, adversarial perturbations, and forgetting in sequential learning settings. We study whether pretrained language models can serve as lightweight auxiliary supervision for vision training without requiring paired image-text data, prompt engineering, or contrastive objectives. Specifically, we evaluate two forms of language guidance, Explicit Language Guidance (ExLG) and Implicit Language Guidance (ImLG). We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across six generalization regimes, including in-distribution, out-of-distribution generalization, shortcut and spurious correlation resistance, texture and shape bias, adversarial robustness, and continual learning. Our analyses show that the two mechanisms have complementary strengths, with explicit guidance consistently benefiting in-distribution, low-data performance, and continual learning retention, while implicit guidance is often more useful in shortcut-sensitive settings and under stronger adversarial perturbations. Importantly, both are lightweight and add minimal parameters and training overhead. The analyses characterize when language-derived structure helps supervised vision training and provides a practical roadmap for using off-the-shelf pretrained models from another modality as auxiliary supervision.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Which Depth Estimator for Jetson AGX Orin? A 2026 Benchmark of Monocular and Stereo Methods
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The Jetson AGX Orin is a common computer for robots and vehicles, yet measured accuracy, speed and energy of current depth estimators on it are hard to find. We benchmark nine model families as of October 2026: the monocular Depth Anything V2 and 3, Depth Pro, MoGe-2, Metric3D v2 and UniDepth V2, and the stereo methods libSGM, NVIDIA ESS and Fast-FoundationStereo. Every method runs on the Orin as a TensorRT FP16 engine or native CUDA code at up to three input sizes, up to the full 5.7 MP, and is scored for metric accuracy against Middlebury 2014 ground truth (non-occluded pixels of the 10 scenes whose disparity stays below 256 px), GPU time, energy and licence. Stereo is far more accurate. At 30 fps, NVIDIA's ESS reaches 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; with more compute, Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33%. The best monocular models reach 12% with the true focal length (Depth Anything 3 Metric-L in 33 ms, Depth Pro in 803 ms), and 3.8-4.0% only with an oracle per-image scale (MoGe-2-L, UniDepth V2-B, Metric3D v2-L). Stereo error falls as the input resolution grows; no monocular model improves, and the metric scale of most drifts away from the truth outside their training resolution. At depth discontinuities, which AbsRel barely registers, the monocular models scatter 17-46% of the edge points between foreground and background, learned stereo 2-9% and libSGM at full resolution 1%. We give recommendations per frame-rate budget and release all code, per-scene results and engine build scripts.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Code and per-scene results: https://github.com/nodarhub/orin-depth-benchmark

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: HarnessIR: Harnessing Multimodal Foundation Models for Universal Real-World Image Restoration
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Real-world low-quality images suffer from complex mixed degradations, including but not limited to noise, blur, atmospheric effects, etc. Recent agentic methods usually model real-world image restoration (Real-IR) as a sequential tool calling problem over task-specific single-degradation restoration models. This paradigm, however, is fundamentally limited because complex real-world degradations cannot be cleanly undone degradation by degradation, and the tool used for task-specific models caps the capability of the agent system. In this work, we present HarnessIR, an agentic framework for Real-IR by harnessing a multimodal foundation model (MFM) as the executor. HarnessIR consists of five stages: perception and diagnosis, on-demand tool invocation, prompt composition, execution, and verification-driven refinement. Unlike prior agentic Real-IR methods that rely on tool chains assembled from task-specific models, HarnessIR feeds the restoration requirements, the perceptual diagnosis, and the evidence into an MFM that performs restoration in a single pass, followed by verification stages to determine whether the result warrants further processing. Under our harness, off-the-shelf MFMs handle restoration tasks remarkably well, achieving state-of-the-art results on the widely used MiO100 synthetic benchmark. More importantly, by exploiting the strong generalization ability of MFMs, HarnessIR delivers compelling restoration quality on challenging real-world scenes where previous agentic IR systems often struggle. Codes is available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HarnessIR.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: StippleDiffusion: Capacity-Constrained Stippling using Controlled Diffusion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Stipple patterns, point sets whose local density tracks a target image, are traditionally produced by per-density iterative optimizers, which are slow, non-differentiable, and must be re-run from scratch for each new target. Learned alternatives have so far addressed only unconditional point generation; capacity-constrained, image-conditioned stippling has remained out of reach. We present the first diffusion-based sampler that simultaneously satisfies a learned local point-distribution prior and a continuous, image-defined capacity constraint at inference. The method is a ControlNet branch built on top of an optimal-transport-grid point-set diffusion baseline, conditioned on the target density map and a high-resolution image. Two design choices make the combination tractable: training and inference are restricted to the late-stage denoising regime, initialized from a density-weighted rejection sample, and the standard zero-convolution injection is replaced with a sigmoid-gated 1x1 projection that preserves the base model's blue-noise structure under hard density signals. A single trained checkpoint accepts arbitrary target densities at inference, generalizes to point budgets that were not seen during training, and produces stipples in time nearly independent of the output point count. On the Icons-50 benchmark, our learned sampler reaches parity with per-density-optimized baselines on every reported metric while remaining differentiable end-to-end.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Appearance Compensation in Volume Rendering
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Can a volume that reproduces every external RGB view still have an incorrect density? We study this question in emission-absorption rendering with an independently parameterized, physically bounded effective source. Appearance compensates a density change by replacing the radiance that it removes from the rest of each ray. We characterize the surviving density information with a shared spatial appearance field. Our first result is an optimal density-only gain after finite-degree spherical-harmonic source refitting. A coupled tensor gauge and physical localized packets identify the sharp limiting nonlinear inverse coefficient as its reciprocal. Our second result realizes positive gain at every fixed finite degree for a residual set of isotropic spatial sources at one fixed density. At the same references, growing angular capacity hides a fixed nonzero density error while retaining physicality and any prescribed finite set of smoothness bounds. Local identifiability and the absence of a capacity-uniform recovery modulus therefore coexist. Our third result constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity: central density doubles and relative density $L^2$ error exceeds $14.52\%$, yet every external RGB ray is unchanged. We connect these continuum results to shared finite representations, continuous pixel measurements and density-sensitive acquisition. Complete-class certificates separate SH0, SH1 and SH2 fits at one learned density.
