The most direct fix, a checker in the trajectory reward, reaches these forks only through fully proportionate trajectories, leaving 74% of GRPO groups with identical rewards and behavior unchanged. This motivates a rethink of where learning signals belong, namely where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. Our method, ForkDPO, contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, at silent forks on both sides of the required behavior. On a test set of unseen repositories, it lowers a 4B model's disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%, against 67.7% for DPO at randomly chosen turns, establishing behavioral divergence as a learning signal for how agents act beyond whether they finish. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Astarojth/silent-forks.

Machine Learning.title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks
Machine Learning.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. To address this issue, we design robust DPO methods that can defend against such attacks. Building on the property that lable flips induce parameter-independent gradient shifts in log-linear DPO, we propose Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which removes the $K$ highest-impact pairs, and Soft-Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which smoothly downweights them. We establish deterministic gradient perturbation bounds uniformly over all attack sets containing at most $K$ flips, explicitly separating defense-induced bias from surviving attack effects. Under bounded-region assumptions, these bounds yield time-uniform parameter and policy deviation guarantees. We further quantify how quadratic regularization improves curvature while introducing additional bias. Experiments on Stanford Human Preferences, HH-RLHF, and UltraFeedback-Binarized validate our analysis.

Machine Learning.title: The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability
Machine Learning.summary: Measuring complexity from a model's own code is biased by failure: a hard prompt can produce a short, broken program that looks simple. We instead score each prompt's structure on six dimensions from the prompt alone, never from generated code or test results. We draw 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater score, and four out-of-panel LLM judges rescore every prompt (composite ICC(2,1) = 0.872). Twenty-one models answer every prompt (105,000 generations), and an independent LLM auditor, checked against known-answer cases, reviews each unit-test verdict. Averaged over models, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 14.0: 83.4% at or below, 90.1% above. That jump is not a law of difficulty: with task-type fixed effects the breakpoint stays at 14.0 but the adjusted jump shrinks from 6.8 to 0.4 points, and neither of the benchmark's two prompt sources reproduces it on its own. Nineteen models pass more often above their own breakpoint and two less often; one of those declines comes from API calls that returned nothing. In post hoc follow-up, Kimi K2.5 shows the clearest decline, at 14.25, under a prompt-source control and within the later source alone. Among failed generations with measurable output complexity, 25.0% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity of at most 10, twice the share among passing ones. The pooled breakpoint moves to 11.25 on raw test outcomes. Human agreement with the index is moderate, paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve its ordering, and overidentification tests reject the six dimensions as instruments, so we make no causal claim. The contribution is a prompt-side way to locate where each model's pass rate changes and to test how much that depends on the prompt mix and on how success is scored.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 24 pages, 6 figures. Code: https://github.com/uwm-se/ComplexityKink ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/uwm-software-engineering/complexity-kink-research

Machine Learning.title: Approximation Theory of Laplacian-Based Neural Operators for Reaction-Diffusion System
Machine Learning.summary: Neural operators provide a framework for learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling efficient surrogate modeling for complex systems. While universal approximation results are now well understood, quantitative approximation analysis specific to nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems remains limited. In this paper, we study Laplacian-based neural operators applied to the solution mapping from initial conditions to time-dependent solutions of nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. By exploiting the Laplacian spectral representation of the diffusion semigroup, we obtain polynomial complexity bounds on the network depth, width, and spectral rank, demonstrating that Laplacian eigenfunction-based neural operators can exploit the structure of the underlying PDE while avoiding the curse of parametric complexity encountered in generic operator learning. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the benefit of Laplacian eigenfunction representations compared with Fourier-based spectral representations.

Machine Learning.title: LowNet: Looped Wavelet Neural Networks with 24 Learnable Parameters for Solving Poisson Equations
Machine Learning.summary: Poisson equations frequently appear in various fields, such as mathematics, physics and informatics. Solving Poisson equation, however, is challenging. Traditional methods are not data-specific, although have high certainty. They require a large number of iterations due to the CFL numerical stability. In contrast, deep learning methods are data-driven and more efficient, but require accurate training data and suffer from heavy computation. To tackle these issues, we propose a wavelet-inspired Poisson solver with 24 trainable scalars. The proposed network has several advantages. First, it is compact. It has four independent $5\times5$ kernels, each represented by six parameters, leading to 24 scalars in total. Such compact format can be deployed on most devices. Second, thanks to the loop design, it achieves higher accuracy than previous methods. A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without increasing its parameters. Numerical experiments confirm that such loop indeed improves the solving accuracy. On 10000 images, one, two, and three loops of the wavelet block lead to PSNRs of $47.27$, $74.14$, and $100.74$ dB, respectively. Third, the proposed method is computationally fast. Thanks to the wavelet transform, the proposed method has linear computation complexity, leading to high computation performance. In short, we propose a novel looped wavelet neural network with compactness, accuracy and efficiency for solving Poisson equations. Our method can be applied in various fields, such as computational fluid dynamics, image reconstruction, biomedical engineering, electromagnetic field simulation.

Machine Learning.title: T-MUON: Tensorizing Muon via t-SVD for Large Language Model Pre-training
Machine Learning.summary: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large language model pretraining by exploiting matrix structure through polar orthogonalization. However, it processes each parameter matrix independently, whereas recent tensor-aware extensions of Muon jointly update groups of eligible matrix parameters through matrix unfoldings. In contrast, we propose T-MUON, a t-SVD-based generalization that groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defines the corresponding Muon-style update directly through the $M$-transform. We show that the exact T-MUON update is a steepest-descent direction under the $\star_M$-spectral norm and establish a convergence guarantee. Across GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M to 1.3B parameters trained on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu, head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform consistently achieves lower validation perplexity than AdamW, Muon, and variants using DFT, DCT, or DST transforms. These gains persist in additional experiments with longer context lengths and larger token budgets, although the preferred tensorization mode varies across settings.

Machine Learning.title: MLFont: Machine Learning-Driven Font Subsetting and Range-Compact Unicode-Range Slicing for Low-Latency Web Typography
Machine Learning.summary:
CSS3 @font-face rules with unicode-range descriptors partition web fonts into downloadable slices. While Latin fonts need ~20 KB in WOFF2, Pan-European (LGC) and East Asian (CJK) fonts contain 2,297-30,759 codepoints (158 KB-5.9 MB in WOFF2), where heuristic partitioning causes unused-glyph downloads, high HTTP RTT, CSS bloat, or missing-glyph fallbacks. We present MLFont, a machine learning and optimization framework that learns font slicing strategies from corpora via three stages: (1) a Zipfian High-Frequency Tier (most) isolating top-frequency codepoints; (2) a Latent Co-Occurrence Topic Tier using Online Variational Bayes LDA (Online LDA) or a Deep Neural Network Topic Model (DNNTM) with Shannon Entropy Difference Loss and Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization; and (3) a Memetic Range-Compact Genetic Algorithm (GA) with Potts-Viterbi dynamic programming and island bridging that minimizes topic discrepancy and CSS fragmentation. Across five Google Noto fonts (LGC, KR, JP, TC, SC), MLFont cuts 3G per-glyph latency by 56.7%-75.3% over single-file delivery and 46.1%-66.3% over equal-bin baselines on CJK with 100% coverage, reduces CSS intervals by 17.9%-41.7%, and achieves 1.56x-6.09x cold-cache speedups (65.4%-84.9% CJK and 44.7% LGC bandwidth savings) across 20 websites in simulator and Headless Chrome benchmarks (45/45 exact slice-set parity).
  Code: https://github.com/wq2012/mlfont
  Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/mlfont

Machine Learning.title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
Machine Learning.summary: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to INFOCOM

Machine Learning.title: Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
Machine Learning.summary: LLM planning research has traditionally focused on discrete-state domains, where actions form a finite, enumerable set. Existing LLM planning frameworks largely assume actions are enumerable, modeling planning as a search process over candidate actions. However, in continuous-state domains, where actions form a continuum and cannot be enumerated, this assumption breaks down. We find a remedy in Newell and Simon's Means-Ends Analysis (MEA), a general problem-solving technique rooted in heuristics from human psychology. We develop Medaka, an MEA-inspired structured prompting framework that encourages recursive goal decomposition, algebraic derivation, and per-step state tracking. To evaluate native LLM planning abilities in continuous-state domains, we develop Liquidworld, a systematic testbed on liquid mixing. On Liquidworld, Medaka can improve performance across model families, suggesting that classical means-ends analysis elicits LLM-native reasoning abilities that are helpful for continuous-state planning.

Machine Learning.title: WILSON - Multi-magnification composites as a foundation for patient-level pathology analysis and diagnostic text generation
Machine Learning.summary: Pathologists examine tissue sections across multiple magnifications and slides, integrating morphological information to establish a diagnosis. In contrast, most pathology foundation models encode thousands of image patches from a single representative ("best") slide and aggregate their features, limiting multiscale and patient-level contextual integration. Here we introduce WILSON, a vision-language foundation model that represents whole-slide images and multi-slide cases through multi-magnification composites. Trained on approximately 189,000 slides spanning 42 organs and 838 diagnostic entities, WILSON enables patient-level analysis, multimodal retrieval and diagnostic text generation. Without task-specific training, WILSON outperformed a dedicated case-level model (macro-F1, 0.52 versus 0.38) and matched substantially larger slide-level models while requiring 400-1,350 times fewer computational operations. End-to-end fine-tuning improved breast cancer subtyping and stromal lymphocyte grading. WILSON also surpassed PRISM in image-text retrieval (recall@1, 75.6% versus 58.1%) and generated diagnostic descriptions that received higher ratings from five board-certified pathologists than competing models. These findings demonstrate that compact, multiscale representations can support computationally efficient, clinically grounded pathology foundation models.
Machine Learning.comment: 61 pages, 6 main figures, with 11 additional figures and 29 tables in the appendices

Machine Learning.title: DF-PALM: Dynamic Fusion Prompt Learning for Audio--Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Few-shot audio classification requires audio--language models to distinguish variable acoustic events from limited labeled data. PALM's main formulation adapts encoded class representations without changing pretrained encoders, but its class representations remain input-independent and classification uses audio features without class-conditioned refinement. We introduce DF-PALM, a dynamic feature-space prompting framework that combines audio-conditioned class representations with asymmetric cross-attention for audio refinement. Class representations are conditioned after text encoding, held fixed across fusion layers for each input, and reused for final scoring. Both pretrained encoders remain frozen, avoiding audio-conditioned text-encoder passes. With PENGI as the frozen backbone, the main 16-shot evaluation covered 11 benchmarks and six baselines. DF-PALM achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro-averaged F1, exceeding PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively. Paired benchmark-level tests supported both gains after Holm correction. Across four shot settings, DF-PALM achieved the highest mean accuracy and macro-averaged F1 among the four evaluated prompt-learning methods. The gains extended to LAION-CLAP and OpenFLAM, with significant improvements over PALM in both metrics. At 50 candidate classes, operator-counted inference floating-point operations increased by 0.39% relative to PALM. These results support instance-conditioned feature-space adaptation as an effective approach to few-shot audio classification. Our code is publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/sunyulin0421/DF-PALM.

Machine Learning.title: Transformers Learn Two Competing Sorting Algorithms, and Only One Length-Generalizes
Machine Learning.summary: We show that two-layer transformers trained to near-zero loss on a sorting task converge to one of two mechanistically distinct solution classes depending on their initialization. One solution class consists of solutions that do not use the second attention layer to sort, but also fail to length-generalize. The other, which uses both attention layers, length-generalizes perfectly, despite only being trained to sort sequences of a fixed length. By carefully choosing the weight initialization, we demonstrate that we can steer the model toward learning one solution or the other. We identify input types that are rare at the training length but increasingly common at longer sequence lengths as a source of this disparity in length-generalization, and find that layer-wise specialization of the second class of solutions allows them to handle these rare sequences more accurately. In the second class, we discover a mechanism by which the second layer attention can use the contextual information gathered by the first layer attention to reduce its search space. On the related task of finding the minimum of a sequence, we find a similar two solution-type phenomenon, but with the opposite generalization pattern, where a different form of layer-wise specialization causes the two-layer solution to length-generalize worse than the single-attention solution.

Machine Learning.title: SZED at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multi-Task Label-Attention and Cross-Modal Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
Machine Learning.summary: We present SZED's submission to ArGuard 2026 Track A: Arabic hateful meme detection. The task has two parts: binary classification (A1) and fine-grained multi-label tagging (A2). For A1, we fuse MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings, comparing concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads. For A2, we use a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and an auxiliary head for cascade calibration. We reach macro-F1 = 0.7597 on A1 and 0.3142 on A2 (averaged over 10 active classes). We report reproducibility across runs, per-class error patterns, and the effect of cascade calibration on the long-tailed A2 label space.

Machine Learning.title: ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision
Machine Learning.summary: Large language model post-training generates self-generated rollouts through reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation, yet this experience is often treated as stale once the policy advances. Historical rollouts can remain compatible with a later policy while preserving behaviors that the policy no longer expresses reliably. However, they may also contain mistakes, abandoned attempts, and redundant actions that should not be imitated, motivating finer-grained selective supervision. We introduce ROSS (Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision), which preserves the full historical trajectory as context while applying loss only to selected model-generated continuations. Across domain-specific reinforcement learning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and agentic reinforcement learning, ROSS consistently improves upstream checkpoints and outperforms baselines across mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and software engineering. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ROSS improves the six-benchmark MOPD average from 58.40% to 62.20% and SWE-bench Verified from 64.20% to 68.40%. These results show that self-rollout training leaves behind reusable behavioral experience that can yield further gains through offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), without additional policy rollouts.

Machine Learning.title: When Weak Submodularity Meets Matroids: How Does Standard Greedy Behave?
Machine Learning.summary:
Weakly submodular maximization finds numerous applications in machine learning, data mining and statistics. In particular, under a cardinality constraint, the standard greedy algorithm is known to attain the tight $(1-e^{-γ})$-approximation guarantee, where $γ$ denotes the submodularity ratio. However, when considering general matroid constraints, \emph{how well standard greedy can perform} has remained a longstanding open question. In this paper, we resolve this question by studying the worst-case approximation guarantee $R_{\mathrm{gr}}(γ,r)$ of standard forward greedy, where $r$ is the rank of matroid. Specifically, our first contribution is the following refined lower bound \begin{equation*} R_{\gr}(γ,r)\ge \max\left\{ \fracγ{r}, \frac{γ^2} {B_γ+\sqrt{γ(r-1)}}, \frac{γ^{r+1}} {2-γ+γ^{r+1}}, \frac{γ^2} {14\left(B_γ+\sqrt{γ(1-γ)(r-1)}\right)} \right\}, \end{equation*} where $B_γ\triangleq2-γ+γ^2$. This lower bound not only strictly improves upon the previous guarantee of $0.4γ^2/(1+\sqrt{γr})$, but also can recover the classical $1/2$-approximation guarantee at $γ=1$. Subsequently, a corresponding upper bound is established for $R_{\mathrm{gr}}(γ,r)$, namely, \begin{equation}\label{eq_upper_abstract} R_{\gr}(γ,r) \le\min\left\{\frac{1}{2},20\max\left\{\fracγ{r}, \frac{γ^2}{B_γ+ \sqrt{γ(1-γ)(r-1)}}\right\}\right\}. \end{equation} For every fixed $γ\in(0,1)$, this Eq.\eqref{eq_upper_abstract} effectively sharpens the recent $O_γ(1/\log(n-1))$ upper bound to $O_γ(r^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the size of ground set. Putting all these results together, we eventually can obtain \[R_{\gr}(γ,r) =
Θ\!\left( \max\left\{\fracγ{r}, \frac{γ^2} {1+\sqrt{γ(1-γ)r}}\right\} \right).\]

Machine Learning.title: FoundPDE: A generative foundation model for data-driven symbolic discovery of partial differential equations
Machine Learning.summary: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observed data is a central inverse problem in computational science and engineering: the goal is not only to predict trajectories, but to identify interpretable symbolic laws that can be analyzed and reused. Existing PDE discovery methods often depend on hand-designed libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, or per-equation symbolic search, making them fragile under sparse observations, noisy data, broad equation families, and unseen symbolic compositions. Here, we introduce FoundPDE, a pretrained data-to-symbol foundation model for PDE discovery. FoundPDE maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectories to symbolic equations with a transformer, uses Fourier and first-order spatial-derivative augmentation to expose complementary trajectory information, refines numerical coefficients, and supports downstream extension with improved generalization through few-shot fine-tuning and hierarchical discovery. On a clean in-domain benchmark spanning 20 PDE families, our model reaches 97.50% type recognition. Under coefficient shifts beyond the training support, type recognition remains 90.53%; under multiplicative Gaussian noise on the model input, it is 94.43% at a 2% noise level but falls to 52.09% at 10%. For unseen composite equations, few-shot fine-tuning reaches over 90% exact recovery on four held-out families, and we further develop a hierarchical discovery algorithm that recovers two-term composites without fine-tuning FoundPDE. By amortizing symbolic discovery across equation families, FoundPDE shifts PDE discovery from per-dataset search toward a reusable pretrained model that extends to new physics with limited additional data, a step toward foundation models that uncover interpretable governing laws directly from scientific data.

Machine Learning.title: Dynamic System Inspired Continuous Large Language Model for AI4Science Tasks
Machine Learning.summary: Scientific foundation models increasingly operate on continuous phenomena, yet still use discrete residual computation. We ask whether pretrained residual transformations can support additional latent computation without expanding the backbone. To test this possibility, we introduce Continuum-LM, which reuses these transformations as dynamical operators in a continuous-depth language model. Its hidden states evolve through an ordinary differential equation evaluated by higher-order numerical integration, with solver order and step size controlling computation. Across eight scientific tasks, Continuum-LM trains stably and improves mean exact-match accuracy by 7.77 and 10.96 percentage points over discrete counterparts at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales, respectively. At 0.6B, it also outperforms an Ouro-style recurrent control under matched parameter and residual-function evaluation budgets. Together, these results support extensible computational depth through parameter reuse, identifying continuous hidden-state evolution as a practical design dimension for scientific language models beyond parameter scaling.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Policy Discrepancy: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates domain specialists into a shared student, but determining how strongly each teacher should supervise remains challenging. Existing discrepancy-based allocation can assign strong supervision even when the student already matches or exceeds the teacher's task performance, since behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit. We propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), which combines specialist merging with capability-guided allocation to account for what the student has already learned. CA-MOPD first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher--student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Supervision decreases as capability gaps close and increases when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. Controlled comparisons further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.

Machine Learning.title: Quadratic Sample Complexity for Strictly Replicable Realizable Learning with Unknown Marginals
Machine Learning.summary: Under the quantifier $\exists A\,\forall D$, where the realizable distribution and its marginal are unknown, we determine the finite-class sample-complexity exponent for strict replicability: two independent samples and one shared seed must produce identical functions. For $\varepsilon=δ=ρ=10^{-4}$, the worst case over $|H|\le M$ is $Θ((\log M)^2)$, without iterated logarithms. For $d\ge1$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/16$, and $0<δ,ρ\le10^{-3}$, every randomized, possibly improper learner valid throughout an explicit anchored realizable family requires $Ω(d^2/(\varepsilonρ^2))$ samples. For the full Boolean class $P_d$, $d\ge2$, in the same parameter range, we prove the matching characterization $Θ(d^2/(\varepsilonρ^2)+\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/δ))$ using a proper Poissonized ball-sampling algorithm. We also give an explicit proper Gibbs upper bound for every finite measurable Boolean class. Our lower bound uses square-root probabilities and volumetric packing; the Gibbs proof builds on established coupling and generalization identities. Finally, we characterize the known-marginal worst case for $P_d$, showing why that interface must be kept distinct.

Multimedia.title: MixiSpeech: Progressive State Distillation for One-Step Vietnamese TTS
Multimedia.summary: Conditional-flow text-to-speech (TTS) models can achieve high synthesis quality with relatively few sampling steps, but collapsing the remaining trajectory to a single update can still cause substantial quality degradation. We propose MixiSpeech, a progressive state distillation framework that converts a multi-step conditional-flow acoustic model into a one-step generator while preserving its architecture and speaker conditioning. Rather than training the one-step model directly, MixiSpeech progressively reduces the global sampling budget through a 10-4-2-1 curriculum, with each student trained to match local teacher-integration endpoints using a masked state-matching objective. We instantiate the framework on a 710-speaker Vietnamese Matcha-TTS model trained from scratch on PhoAudiobook. On 100 shared test text-speaker pairs, direct one-step inference substantially degrades synthesis quality, obtaining 1.6846 UTMOS22-Strong and 6.21% WER compared with 2.2923 and 4.65% for the 10-step teacher. In contrast, the distilled one-step model achieves 2.2678 UTMOS22-Strong, 4.63% WER, and 2.83% CER, recovering most of the quality lost at the one-step operating point while requiring only a single acoustic vector-field evaluation. End-to-end inference time decreases from 0.0662 s for the 10-step teacher to 0.0312 s for MixiSpeech, corresponding to a 2.12 measured speedup. These results show that progressive state distillation can make one-step conditional-flow TTS practical without relying on a large multi-step sampling budget. Project page: https://mixispeech.solanai.us/
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at SOICT2026

Multimedia.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
Multimedia.summary: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.

Multimedia.title: Evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models on Spoken Sarcasm Detection
Multimedia.summary: Sarcasm detection remains challenging because sarcastic intent often depends on information across text, speech, and vision. We systematically evaluate large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) for sarcasm detection on English (MUStARD++) and Chinese (MCSD), considering both feature-extraction settings and direct classification. In the feature-extraction settings, audio provides the strongest unimodal performance on both datasets, while multimodal fusion shows dataset-dependent benefits. In direct classification, Qwen2.5-Omni achieves the strongest zero-shot performance among the evaluated models, with further substantial gains after fine-tuning. Error analysis further shows that additional modalities can both correct and introduce errors, highlighting the need for selective multimodal integration.

Multimedia.title: AffordanceVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model Empowering Action Generation through Affordance-Aware Understanding
Multimedia.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models leverage the rich world knowledge of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to enable instruction-following robotic manipulation. However, the structural mismatch between VLM semantic spaces and embodied control policies often hinders the learning of precise perception-action mappings. To address this challenge, we propose AffordanceVLA, a scalable, unified framework that introduces structured affordance learning as a task-oriented and object-centric intermediate representation to establish a more precise and robust perception-action mapping. Specifically, we progressively model manipulation priors through three complementary components - Which2Act, Where2Act, and How2Act - which jointly produce spatially grounded, semantically conditioned, and action-coupled intermediate representations, thereby naturally bridging vision, language, and action. We integrate these modules into a Mixture-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture and adopt a three-stage progressive training curriculum that leverages 8.8M affordance-centric grounding and pointing samples, translating scalable vision-language supervision into improved robotic manipulation. To overcome the scarcity of dense affordance labels in robotic datasets, we also develop a robust automated data augmentation pipeline. Extensive experiments on ID & OOD simulation and real-world demonstrate that AffordanceVLA outperforms strong VLA baselines across diverse manipulation scenarios, validating structured affordance learning as a scalable and robust bridge that integrates multi-source vision-language supervision while connecting pretrained VLM semantics to embodied robot control.
Multimedia.comment: 37 pages, 9 figures, including supplementary material. Updated references and formatting. Project page: https://skywalker-yqz.github.io/AffordanceVLA/ Code: https://github.com/Skywalker-yqz/AffordanceVLA

Multimedia.title: Re:Cognize -- A Framework For Open-Set Comic Character Re-Identification
Multimedia.summary: Comics and manga tell stories through characters whose appearances change from panel to panel, yet readers recognise them hundreds of pages later without ever consulting a cast list. Character re-identification models rarely face the same challenge: existing evaluations give them a fixed set of identities before the story begins. \textbf{Re:Cognize} instead asks models to recognise characters as the story unfolds and learn who is who along the way. Across three manga corpora, we evaluate five Re-ID backbones and \textbf{MECHA}, a memory-augmented baseline we introduce, and find that the central difficulty lies somewhere unexpected. Recognising familiar characters is nearly solved. Knowing which matches to trust is not. When models build a gallery and grow it from their own predictions, their performance deteriorates, even though correct identity labels would improve it by over twenty points. This raises a simple question: when should a model trust its own match? We derive a single comparison that determines when gallery updates improve recognition and use it to design \textbf{VOUCH}, which updates its memory only when the page provides supporting evidence. Without fitting additional parameters, VOUCH recovers between one-third and two-thirds of the improvement available from perfect labels. RE:COGNIZE measures whether a model can recognise characters as it reads; VOUCH shows how to remember them reliably. We focus our methodological claims on identity maintenance for previously encountered characters, while separately evaluating new-character emergence as a diagnostic under a fixed reference rule to distinguish recognition from discovery.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS ED Track, 2026

Multimedia.title: MuSP-Bench: Advanced Multimodal Benchmarking of Music Understanding across Score and Performance
Multimedia.summary: Musicians commonly communicate musical intent through scores and performances. To investigate whether models can reason across both modalities, we introduce MuSP-Bench, a human-authored benchmark of 490 questions assessing understanding across Musical Scores and Performances, both individually and in combination. The benchmark spans interpretive and long-horizon reasoning across classical piano and orchestral works, represented through ABC notation, score images, MIDI, and audio. Our evaluation of frontier multimodal large language models reveals substantial difficulties in understanding musical scores and even greater challenges in reasoning about audio. The benchmark is available at https://musp.vaclis.net/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Enhancing Gaze Reasoning in Vision Foundation Models for Gaze Following
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Gaze following requires both scene understanding and gaze reasoning to localize the gaze target of an in-scene person. Recently, vision foundation models (VFMs) have demonstrated strong performance on this task, enabling simpler architectures while outperforming prior methods. However, we observe a key limitation of VFM-based approaches: while VFMs substantially improve scene understanding, they contribute little to gaze reasoning. As a result, existing methods often rely on semantically salient objects rather than true gaze cues, leading to degraded performance when targets are not salient. To address this, we propose a novel training mechanism to enhance gaze reasoning in VFMs for gaze following. Our method includes: (1) a head-conditioned local LoRA, which enables localized adaptation to preserve scene token learning while improving head token learning for gaze reasoning; and (2) an out-of-cone penalty, which injects gaze cues into head tokens while aligning them with scene tokens. Experiments on the GazeFollow and VAT datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong improvements when gaze targets are not semantically salient. Our findings offer valuable insights for advancing future gaze following research. Code will be available at https://github.com/shijing-wang/HCloRA.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PRISM: Feed-Forward Single-Image 3D Reconstruction via Geometric Warp-Residual Modeling
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reconstructing 3D scenes from a single image is a fundamental challenge in computer vision, with broad applications in virtual reality, robotics, and content creation. Recent methods achieve outstanding performance by leveraging camera-controlled video diffusion models, but rely on iterative diffusion sampling, which greatly limits their practical deployment. We observe that geometric forward warping alone can cover the majority of a target view directly from the input image, with only a compact residual left for the encoder to correct. Motivated by this observation, we propose PRISM, a feed-forward framework that decomposes multi-view latent prediction into a parameter-free geometric prior and a learned residual correction, with no diffusion sampling required at inference. To enable generalization from purely synthetic training data, we devise a two-stage training strategy combining latents supervised distillation for geometric generalization and perceptual fine-tuning for appearance quality optimization. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves competitive reconstruction quality compared with diffusion-based methods, while reducing inference time dramatically to only 36 seconds per scene. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/microjie372/PRISM}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Domain Shift in Echocardiography: Interpretable Quantification and Prediction of Cross-Dataset Left Ventricular Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Cross-dataset generalisation remains a major barrier to clinical deployment of echocardiographic left ventricular segmentation, yet the sources of this shift are rarely disentangled. We examined whether transfer degradation could be estimated before deployment using handcrafted ultrasound descriptors, VAE latent features, and segmentation-derived latent features across six echocardiographic datasets. Geometry-aware preprocessing substantially improved several poor transfer cases, suggesting that much of the apparent domain shift reflects field-of-view and framing inconsistencies rather than intrinsic acoustic differences alone. Intensity z-normalisation changed dataset separability by less than 0.005, indicating that brightness and contrast are not the dominant shift axis. Absolute Dice drop on held-out source-target pairs was predicted with an R-squared value of 0.612, an MAE of 0.082, and a Spearman rho of 0.681. The variant without LV and fan-shaped features retained approximately 70% of this explanatory power, supporting mask-free transfer-risk monitoring. The most informative discrepancy measure depended on the representation, with CMD strongest in z-normalised handcrafted features, with an absolute r of approximately 0.86 and an R-squared value of approximately 0.70; log-Wasserstein strongest in VAE space, with an r of approximately -0.90 and an R-squared value of approximately 0.81; and log-MMD strongest in LV-segmentation latent features, with an r of approximately -0.92 and an R-squared value of approximately 0.84. Apparent vendor effects were largely dataset-confounded. Echocardiographic domain shift is therefore structured and measurable, and its impact on segmentation can be partly reduced through geometry-aware preprocessing and anticipated using representation-specific transfer-risk estimation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RePrior: Measurement-Reconciled Prior Correction for Sparse-View CBCT Reconstruction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is severely under-constrained by limited X-ray projections. Learned reconstruction can provide complementary anatomical information, but using it as a prior in patient-specific Gaussian reconstruction introduces two challenges. First, the discrepancy between the learned prior and current reconstruction is spatially non-uniform: some local differences contain useful missing 3D information, whereas others reflect prior bias. Second, even a volumetrically beneficial correction can conflict with the observed X-ray measurements. Since X-ray measurements are line integrals, spatially separated corrections may affect overlapping rays, with their signed projection responses reinforcing or partially canceling in the measurement residual, so their feasibility cannot always be assessed independently. In this paper, we introduce RePrior, a multi-stage progressive prior-correction framework that addresses correction actionability, measurement feasibility, and representation expressivity. Selective Correction Proposal (SCP) first identifies actionable signed local corrections from prior--reconstruction discrepancies. Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation (MCR) then jointly enforces their consistency with patient-specific X-ray measurements, while Hybrid Residual Enhancement (HRE) recovers additional correction capacity through complementary voxel- and Gaussian-domain degrees of freedom around the reconciled anchor. RePrior requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning. RePrior gains approximately 2.6~dB in 3D PSNR over R$^2$-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN. Beyond prior-assisted reconstruction, it delivers additional gains in volumetric quality and observed-view projection fidelity, with consistent gains in held-out-view fidelity in the backbone-matched evaluation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Predicting Individual Differences in Lipreading From Eye-Tracking and Pupillometry During Silent Visual Speech
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Lipreading ability varies widely, including among people who are hard of hearing. Although mouth-directed attention is linked to speechreading outcomes, it remains unclear how much lipreading skill can be inferred from viewing behavior and which signals carry this information. We examine whether individual differences in lipreading ability are reflected in viewing behavior during silent speech and quantify the contributions of gaze dynamics, pupil-linked signals, and spatial viewing allocation. We introduce the Lipreading Perception Study (LiPS) dataset and a tracker-independent preprocessing pipeline that synchronizes SR Research EyeLink gaze and pupil recordings with the stimuli. Twenty-four adults (age 32 $\pm$ 10 years) completed a four-alternative forced-choice silent lipreading task. An extreme-groups protocol yielded 18 participants labeled as stronger or weaker lipreaders. Each participant-trial included four aligned views: lip-region images, frame-level gaze, pupil summaries, and spatial viewing proportions. A four-branch neural network with cross-modal attention predicted labels using participant-disjoint splits and systematic ablations. The full model reached accuracy 0.680 $\pm$ 0.040 across five folds, outperforming naive fusion baselines in accuracy. The pupil and viewing-summary branch was most informative: removing it caused the largest degradation (0.618 accuracy, 0.623 AUC), while it alone achieved 0.675 accuracy. The lip-image stream contributed little to participant-level discrimination. Individual differences in lipreading are reflected in pupil-linked and frame-level gaze signals rather than in how much time a viewer spends looking at the mouth. Synchronized gaze and pupillary measures may provide objective markers of visual speech perception, warranting investigation in larger, clinically diverse populations. LiPS provides a resource for extending this work.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Submitted to the Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. 5 figures, 2 tables

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Multi-Speed Field Evaluation of a Semi-Autonomous Precision Sprayer for Weed Control in Vegetable Crops
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Machine vision-guided precision spraying is promising for sustainable vegetable production by enabling site-specific weed targeting, reducing herbicide application while protecting crop yield and quality. However, the effects of operating speed of sprayer systems on the integrated detection-tracking-actuation pipeline remain insufficiently characterized under field conditions. This study evaluated a semi-autonomous, tractor-based spraying system for targeted weed control in radish and quantified performance across three operating speeds. A five-season dataset comprising 10,599 images and 84,311 annotated instances across seven classes was curated for model development. A YOLOv11-medium model was integrated with ByteTrack tracking and a customized 12-nozzle sprayer on a semi-autonomous electric tractor. Field trials were conducted at 0.13, 0.27, and 0.45 m/s (i.e., 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 mph) to characterize speed-dependent changes in weed detection, targeting, actuation, and crop damage. At the lowest speed of 0.13 m/s, the system achieved 94.6% mAP@50 and 93.2% recall for weed and crop detection. However, increasing platform speed substantially reduced system performance, with weed hit rate declining from 78.3% to 35.0% and crop contact rates increasing from 20.1% to 28.7%. Consequently, the system did not meet predefined commercial-viability thresholds. These results demonstrate that practical deployment requires improvements beyond weed detection alone, particularly coordinated improvements in motion-robust plant perception, spray-timing compensation, and crop-adjacent actuation precision. The identified performance bottlenecks provide specific engineering targets for advancing vision-guided precision spraying toward practical, high-speed vegetable weed management. The software programs developed in this study have been made publicly available to support future precision weeding research.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $ρ\approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($ρ\approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SiLVi: Simple Interface for Labeling Video Interactions
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Computer vision methods are increasingly used for the automated analysis of large volumes of video data collected through camera traps, drones, or direct observations of animals in the wild. While recent advances have focused primarily on detecting individual actions, much less work has addressed the detection and annotation of interactions -- a crucial aspect for understanding social and individualized animal behavior. Existing open-source annotation tools support either behavioral labeling without localization of individuals, or localization without the capacity to capture interactions. To bridge this gap, we present SiLVi, an open-source labeling software that integrates both functionalities. SiLVi enables researchers to annotate behaviors and interactions directly within video data, generating structured outputs suitable for training and validating computer vision models. By linking behavioral ecology with computer vision, SiLVi facilitates the development of automated approaches for fine-grained behavioral analyses. Although developed primarily in the context of animal behavior, SiLVi could be useful more broadly to annotate human interactions in other videos that require extracting dynamic scene graphs. The software, along with documentation and download instructions, is available at: https://silvi.ozankanbertay.com.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Documentation link updated, Linux version added

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SpriteStage: Long Horizon Animation Generation via Progressive Scene Programming and Replay
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: OccSim: Multi-kilometer Simulation with Long-horizon Occupancy World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Data-driven autonomous driving simulation has long been constrained by its heavy reliance on pre-recorded driving logs or spatial priors, such as HD maps. This fundamental dependency severely limits scalability, restricting open-ended generation capabilities to the finite scale of existing collected datasets. To break this bottleneck, we present OccSim, the first 3D occupancy world model driven simulator that requires neither HD maps nor log-derived layouts. OccSim obviates the requirement for continuous logs or HD maps; conditioned only on a single initial frame and a sequence of future ego-actions. It can stably generate over 3000 continuous frames, an 80x improvement in stable generation length over previous SoTA occupancy world models, and fuses them into maps spanning over 9 kilometers. Further qualitative stress tests show that it can roll out beyond 110K frames. OccSim is powered by two modules: W-DiT based static occupancy world model and the Layout Generator. W-DiT handles the ultra-long-horizon generation of static environments by explicitly introducing known rigid transformations in architecture design, while the Layout Generator populates the dynamic foreground with reactive agents based on the synthesized road topology. With these designs, OccSim can synthesize massive, diverse simulation streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate its downstream utility: data collected directly from OccSim can pre-train 4D semantic occupancy forecasting models to achieve up to 67% zero-shot performance on unseen data, outperforming previous asset-based simulator by 11%. When the collected data is scaled up to 5x its original size, zero-shot performance increases to 74%.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PCHMR: Empowering and Benchmarking Human Mesh Recovery in Privacy-Constrained Real-World Settings
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Fine-tuning directly on user-side data is an effective way to improve the performance of widely adopted data-driven human mesh recovery (HMR) models. However, doing so for existing HMR methods often assumes aggregating user-side data from real-world HMR-deployed devices to a central training server, posing a significant privacy risk as sensitive human images are transmitted. How can human mesh recovery be evaluated and improved in privacy-constrained real-world settings? We study this question through a benchmark in which state-of-the-art HMR models are trained with federated learning and a secure-aggregation variant, neither of which centralizes raw images, and evaluated across a wide range of client-scale and data-heterogeneity settings. We document that common HMR training pipelines are built around centralized data access and quantify how representative HMR backbones behave when that assumption is removed. Furthermore, to study the data bottleneck of privacy-constrained HMR training, we propose DePoser, a local annotation and fine-tuning pipeline enhanced with depth foundation models, with which collaboratively trained HMR models can be locally tailored to the end user's distribution. On in-the-wild data, fine-tuning on DePoser annotations improves personalization accuracy, measured against DePoser-generated pseudo-ground truth. This benchmark aims to support future work on privacy-constrained HMR models and their real-world deployment and evaluation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VTF900: A 900-Subject Visible-Thermal Face Recognition Dataset and Benchmark
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Despite advancements in visible-thermal face recognition, where thermal probe (query) face images are matched against visible enrollment templates, existing benchmarks are currently limited by small gallery sizes (N $\approx$ 100 subjects). This limitation inhibits the ability to accurately evaluate visible-thermal facial recognition at scale and to report significant recognition performance metrics, which have better operational relevance. Therefore, we introduce VTF900, a large-scale visible-thermal face recognition benchmark with 900 subjects and paired imagery that includes expression, pose, and occlusion variations. VTF900 is designed to support large-scale (i.e., large gallery) evaluations across verification (1:1 matching) and closed-set identification (1:N matching) for visible-thermal face recognition. Furthermore, VTF900 specifically addresses the challenging combination of cross-spectral and cross-dataset analysis. In this paper, after training models on the ARL-VTF dataset, we provide benchmark analyses across convolutional (baseline), vision transformers, and domain-adaptive neural network architectures to assess how these methods scale. At full gallery scale (N = 900), transformer models achieve strong discriminative performance under frontal conditions (e.g., ViT-B: 97.68% AUC, 51.10% TAR@1%FAR), while domain-adaptive methods such as DPIT-ResNet50 demonstrate greater robustness under off-pose conditions (94.68%AUC, 36.08% TAR@1%FAR). Our results show that high AUC at small scale does not translate to reliable performance at deployment scale, and that pose variation significantly amplifies performance degradation. VTF900 exposes these limitations, enabling more rigorous evaluation of cross-spectral face recognition systems.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Authenticated Contradictions from Desynchronized Provenance and Watermarking
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Cryptographic provenance standards such as C2PA and invisible watermarking are positioned as complementary defenses for content authentication, yet the two verification layers are technically independent: neither conditions on the output of the other. This work formalizes and empirically demonstrates the $\textit{Integrity Clash}$, a condition in which a digital asset carries a cryptographically valid C2PA manifest asserting human authorship while its pixels simultaneously carry a watermark identifying it as AI-generated, with both signals passing their respective verification checks in isolation. We construct metadata washing workflows that produce these authenticated fakes through standard editing pipelines, requiring no cryptographic compromise, only the semantic omission of a single assertion field permitted by the current C2PA specification. To close this gap, we propose a cross-layer audit protocol that jointly evaluates provenance metadata and watermark detection status, achieving 100% classification accuracy across 3,500 test images spanning four conflict-matrix states and three realistic perturbation conditions. Our results demonstrate that the gap between these verification layers is unnecessary and technically straightforward to close.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at CVPR 2026 Workshop Authenticity & Provenance in the Age of AI (APAI)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Stride Independent Patching for Deep Learning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: This paper presents semi-automatic stride-independent patching (SSP) as an alternative to automatic stride-dependent patching techniques. SSP uses user or expert input to position predefined patches over one or more objects of interest. To evaluate its effectiveness, three patch-based datasets were created using SSP, overlapping patching (Overlap), and non-overlapping patching (Noverlap). DeepLabV3+ models with ResNet50, ResNet18, and MobileNetV2 backbones were trained sepa-rately on each dataset. Quantitative evaluations were performed on the respective test splits and a common external test set. SSP generally achieved higher segmentation scores on the test splits and required the shortest model training time across all three backbones. On the external test set, SSP achieved the highest average precision and F1-score across backbones, whereas Noverlap achieved the highest average recall. These preliminary results demonstrate that the potentially greater spatial coverage of Noverlap and Overlap did not generally translate into better segmentation perfor-mance and that SSP offers a favorable balance between segmentation performance and model training time.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SL-Ground: Sentence-Level Grounding for Fine-Grained Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Grounding-based open-vocabulary detectors provide a widely used framework for text-conditioned localization, with a phrase-grounding formulation that aligns object queries to individual text tokens and recovers class scores through token-to-class aggregation. We observe that this token-level scoring design becomes a bottleneck for fine-grained open-vocabulary object detection, where the target category is defined by a complete compositional description rather than by isolated tokens. Based on this observation, we propose SL-Ground, a sentence-level grounding reformulation for grounding-based open-vocabulary detection. Instead of scoring queries against fragmented token evidence, SL-Ground encodes each category description as a complete sentence-level representation and directly scores object queries against these representations. To evaluate fine-grained recognition across label granularity, we construct a multi-granularity Stanford Cars benchmark spanning vehicle type, brand, and car model. At the finest car-model granularity, SL-Ground raises AP over the token-level variant from 14.5 to 70.6 under matched training candidate sampling and to 86.0 with full-vocabulary training, while better preserving open-vocabulary capability and avoiding repeated prompt chunking. Beyond Stanford Cars, SL-Ground also improves FG-OVD performance, achieving the best average AP among compared methods. These results show that sentence-level grounding provides a more suitable scoring unit for fine-grained OVOD and offers a practical path toward fine-grained grounding-based open-vocabulary detectors.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (Conference Papers). 19 pages, 15 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Directionally Factorized Illumination with Spherical Harmonic Rotation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Estimating Individual Tree Height and Species from UAV Imagery
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Accurate estimation of forest biomass, a major carbon sink, relies heavily on tree-level traits such as height and species. Unoccupied Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) capturing high-resolution imagery from a single RGB camera offer a cost-effective and scalable approach for mapping and measuring individual trees. We introduce BIRCH-Trees, the first benchmark for individual tree height and species estimation from tree-centered UAV images, spanning three datasets: temperate forests, tropical forests, and boreal plantations. We also present DINOvTree, a unified approach using a Vision Foundation Model (VFM) backbone with task-specific heads for simultaneous height and species prediction. Through extensive evaluations on BIRCH-Trees, we compare DINOvTree against commonly used vision methods, including VFMs, as well as biological allometric equations. We find that DINOvTree achieves top overall results with accurate height predictions and competitive classification accuracy while using only 54% to 58% of the parameters of the second-best approach.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://RolnickLab.github.io/DINOvTree

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: At FullTilt: Real-Time Open-Set 3D Macromolecule Detection Directly from Tilted 2D Projections
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Open-set 3D macromolecule detection in cryogenic electron tomography eliminates the need for target-specific model retraining. However, strict VRAM constraints prohibit processing an entire 3D tomogram, forcing current methods to rely on slow sliding-window inference over extracted subvolumes. To overcome this, we propose FullTilt, an end-to-end framework that redefines 3D detection by operating directly on aligned 2D tilt-series. Because a tilt-series contains significantly fewer images than slices in a reconstructed tomogram, FullTilt eliminates redundant volumetric computation, accelerating inference by orders of magnitude. To process the entire tilt-series simultaneously, we introduce a tilt-series encoder to efficiently fuse cross-view information. We further propose a multiclass visual prompt encoder for flexible prompting, a tilt-aware query initializer to effectively anchor 3D queries, and an auxiliary geometric primitives module to enhance the model's understanding of multi-view geometry while improving robustness to adverse imaging artifacts. Extensive evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that FullTilt achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while drastically reducing runtime and VRAM requirements, paving the way for rapid, large-scale visual proteomics analysis. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Kaminyou/FullTilt.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UniAVC: Unified Audio-Video Creation via Progressive Training and Asymmetric Scheduling
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Page: https://hkust-longgroup.github.io/UniAVC; Code: https://github.com/HKUST-LongGroup/UniAVC; Note: Abstract is shortened to meet arXiv's characters limitation

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Video-Language Entailment for Video Similarity Estimation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Comparing videos to assess their semantic similarity remains a challenging task for current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which are primarily trained with single-video objectives. While most prior works have focused on computing global similarity, recent studies have introduced the more challenging problem of concept-based similarity, which measures how similar two videos are with respect to specific concepts (e.g., activity, location). However, no dedicated approaches have yet leveraged LMMs to explicitly address this task. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap introducing Video Caption Entailment for video similarity estimation (VICE): a dual-branch design that leverages LMMs for cross-video reasoning. Each branch jointly processes one video and the caption of the other, measuring their alignment for a specific concept via video-language entailment. The outputs from both branches are fused to produce a final similarity score, along with a textual explanation of the model reasoning. This approach leverages the model's native single-video understanding while enabling fine-grained comparative reasoning between video and text. Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show that VICE outperforms models that process both videos simultaneously, highlighting the promise of single-video reasoning for concept-based similarity estimation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ATLAS: Learning to Adapt LVLM Attention for Reasoning Video Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to localize and segment objects referred to by natural-language expressions throughout a video. Although large vision-language models (LVLMs) implicitly encode localization cues in their attention maps, these attentions are often noisy, diffuse, and scattered across layers, heads, and modalities, limiting their direct use for segmentation. Existing methods typically rely on handcrafted attention-selection heuristics or computationally expensive attention refinement. We propose ATLAS, an attention adaptation framework that learns to transform raw LVLM attentions into object-centric localization cues. ATLAS treats attentions from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features, combining high-resolution frame-level attentions that capture spatial information with low-resolution video-level attentions that encode temporal context. A lightweight U-Net equipped with temporal attention and FiLM-based modulation fuses these complementary representations to generate coarse segmentation heatmaps, which are propagated across the video using SAM2. Extensive experiments on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks show that ATLAS outperforms existing frozen-backbone methods. Code and models are available at \url{https://hamidreza-136.github.io/atlas/}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Evidence Field: Adaptive Covering Programs for Medical Imaging
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Medical image classifiers typically return predictions without a native contract for independently reconstructing their spatial decision computation. Evidence Field is a trainable spatial-program architecture that jointly produces class scores, selected covering programs and signed evidence. Its encoder combines absolute and image-relative response fields with associative spatial moments and learned characteristic sums. A typed classifier scores individual regions and parent-conditioned multiplicative groups; a covering recursion selects scale, partition and composition. We establish exact one-fold coverage, optimality within the registered grammar, a bound relating smooth training to hard inference, signed-score conservation and class-centred offset invariance. Direct contractions and their adjoint specify arithmetic and storage scaling on two- and three-dimensional grids. Native output records bind inputs, parameters, supports, types and contextual dependencies to individual and ensemble predictions. In a separately reported histopathology application, patient-separated training and evaluation across held-out centres provide empirical evidence for the architecture. Trained mechanism and corrected-loss comparisons distinguish predictive effects from implementation correctness; independent readers reconstruct descriptors, routes, scores and probability mixtures. The principal contribution is a coupled representation, decision and evidence architecture whose selected computation can be reproduced independently.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Design Anything, Design at Scale
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: As multimodal resources are transformed into media outputs, agentic AI is expected to stay aligned with design intent over long horizons. Designers follow briefs specifying goals, constraints, and deliverables, with later work building on earlier decisions. Recent work reuses design experience across tasks, yet alignment among artifacts within one project remains challenging. Agents therefore need to preserve and apply this intent across domains and as projects grow. We introduce Design Anything, a graph-based harness that preserves design intent outside the model and binds deliverables to the workflow steps that produce them through an intent-execution graph.
