However, most existing methods assume that amplitude and phase can be restored independently, while overlooking their inherent spectral coupling. This artificial decoupling often leads to information inconsistency and structural distortions. To address this issue, we propose a frequency-spatial framework that jointly models spectral interaction and reliable prior guidance. We first empirically analyze the coupling between amplitude and phase and develop an Amplitude-Phase Adaptive Compensation Fusion (APACF) module. Instead of enforcing a hard separation between the two components, APACF enables their bidirectional interaction, resulting in spectrally coherent restoration. In addition, directly extracting priors from raw low-light inputs is unreliable, since severe noise and underexposure destroy critical visual content. To alleviate this problem, we introduce an Endogenous Reliability Prior (ERP). Specifically, we treat an intermediate result, preliminarily restored in the frequency domain and already close to the ground-truth illumination, as a high-fidelity source for extracting complementary pseudo-infrared and gradient cues. Based on ERP, we further design a Dual-Modal Guided Refinement Network (DGRN) to inject these purified structural cues into the decoder, thereby recovering missing fine textures more accurately. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently surpasses existing methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/bywlzts/Amplitude-Phase-Coupling-Net.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: O-SCD++: Replay-Free Online Scene Change Detection via Recursive Evidence Fusion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Online scene change detection requires an agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than its offline counterpart, and online methods have consistently trailed offline accuracy. O-SCD closed that gap by treating change as a persistent property of a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene, surpassing the strongest offline methods in change detection accuracy while operating at over 10 frames per second. O-SCD optimizes a change field over the Gaussians of the reference map, refitting it to all past cue maps at every frame, a step that consumes more than half of the per-frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present a replay-free formulation that eliminates this trade-off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians directly, by a single backward pass of the renderer, which reduces multi-view fusion to an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. The self-supervised objective that O-SCD minimizes by descent also determines the decision threshold exactly, by sorting, yielding a label-free per-frame cutoff whose margin provides a selective-prediction signal. On PASLCD, our method improves mean intersection over union from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 frames per second, even exceeding O-SCD's offline result while remaining strictly causal.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 29 pages, 14 figures, 16 tables. Project page: https://jjunsss.github.io/HumanSkill-4D/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: BodyBridge: Grounded Body Layers for Sim-to-Real Translation of Vulnerable Road Users
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Simulation-to-real driving video diffusion models can translate photorealistic scenes, but they typically represent pedestrians and cyclists, vulnerable road users (VRUs), as generic object classes. This is insufficient for vulnerable road users whose safety-relevant appearance depends on articulated pose and identity. We present BodyBridge and Grounded Body Layers (GBL), a simulator-derived, pixel-aligned representation that combines scene geometry, canonical per-pixel body correspondence, and exact VRU masks. GBL provides explicit articulation to the video diffusion model, emphasizes VRU regions during control-branch post-training, and supports additive composition with scene-geometry control at inference. It also enables per-joint evaluation of generated VRUs and a failure taxonomy for identity errors. On CARLA-to-real translation, BodyBridge improves near-range PCK@0.5 by 22% over the released depth-conditioned baseline. Replacing normal-map body control with canonical correspondence reduces body flips by 18%, while composition reduces near-range facing flips by 27%. These results show that explicit body grounding complements scene-level control and improves pose-faithful VRU generation. All code, data, and model checkpoints will be made publicly available to support reproducible, pedestrian-aware autonomous driving research.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Shape Distribution Matters: Shape-Specific Mixture-of-Experts for Amodal Segmentation Under Diverse Occlusions
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Amodal segmentation aims to predict complete object masks covering both visible and occluded regions, serving as a critical foundation for robust multimedia scene understanding and interactive media editing. This task poses significant challenges in complex visual media due to severe occlusions and extreme shape variation, ranging from rigid furniture to highly deformable clothing. Existing one-size-fits-all approaches struggle to reason about diverse amodal shapes in multimedia content due to limited representation capacity. While a mixture-of-experts framework is a natural solution, naively applying it without considering the underlying shape distribution leads to mismatched routing and redundant experts. To address these issues, we introduce ShapeMoE, a shape-specific sparse mixture-of-experts framework designed for complex visual scene parsing. The key idea is to learn a latent shape distribution space and dynamically route each object to a lightweight expert tailored to its geometric characteristics. Specifically, ShapeMoE encodes each object into a compact Gaussian embedding that captures key shape features. A Shape-Aware Sparse Router then maps the object to the most suitable expert, enabling precise shape-aware routing. Each expert is lightweight and specializes in recovering occluded regions for specific shape patterns. ShapeMoE is designed for shape-specific expert specialization while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate that ShapeMoE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Beyond advancing fundamental visual reasoning, ShapeMoE provides a robust and efficient visual prior for downstream multimedia applications, particularly in occlusion-heavy immersive environments.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MLLM-Guided Autonomous Object Detection for Open-World Understanding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Object detection typically relies on predefined category vocabularies, while open-world and open-vocabulary approaches remain limited by generic unknown labels or externally specified detection concepts. We propose LAOD, an MLLM-Guided Autonomous Object Detection framework in which a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) generates an image-specific detection vocabulary that is grounded by an open-vocabulary detector. This decomposition separates semantic concept discovery from spatial localization and removes the need to manually enumerate target categories at inference time. We evaluate LAOD using Class-Agnostic Average Precision (CAAP), Semantic Naming Average Precision (SNAP), and Semantic Localization Average Precision (SemLoc-AP), which measure localization, semantic naming, and their correct association, respectively. Experiments on COCO-Val, LVIS-minival, and COCO-OOD across multiple MLLMs and detectors demonstrate strong performance across common, long-tailed, and out-of-distribution objects, while showing that grounding quality remains a major determinant of end-to-end performance. LAOD also substantially outperforms both direct MLLM-based object detection and dedicated models trained specifically for open-ended detection. Overall, the results support a modular formulation of autonomous object detection in which MLLMs determine what to detect and specialized open-vocabulary detectors determine where those concepts occur.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: S3D-Mosaic: Subgradient-Guided Cross-Band Structure Transfer for Spectral Demosaicing
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multispectral filter array (MSFA) imaging enables snapshot spectral acquisition, but its per-band sparse sampling causes severe spatial aliasing. Although missing spatial structures can be inferred across bands, wavelength-dependent contrast variations make direct cross-band transfer unreliable. Existing model-based methods lack explicit magnitude-invariant mechanisms, and learning-based methods require layout-specific training or per-image tuning, limiting generalization. To address these issues, we propose S3D-Mosaic, a model-based spectral demosaicing method built upon a subgradient-guided cross-band structure transfer framework. We first establish a subgradient-guided regularization framework with a generalized cosine-similarity interpretation, providing a convex mechanism for magnitude-invariant information transfer. Then we design a compact Directional Sparse Equivariant Difference Convolution (DSE-DConv) for band-level extraction of orientation-selective, high-frequency structure features at low computational cost. Instantiating the framework with DSE-DConv on spectrally adjacent bands yields a cross-band self-structure similarity regularizer for spectral demosaicing, which we optimize via a dual-scan ADMM algorithm that decouples the bidirectional dependency while propagating magnitude-robust structural information across bands. With DSE-DConv's two parameters trained once via self-supervision, S3D-Mosaic outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on CAVE and NTIRE 2022, and generalizes robustly to varying MSFA layouts, pan-mosaic fusion, and real-world UAV data with fixed reconstruction hyperparameters. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/bestwishes43/S3D-Mosaic}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ZeroDSS: Semantic Segmentation from Class Names Alone
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Semantic segmentation depends heavily on real images with pixel-level annotations, making dense supervision a major obstacle to deployment in new domains. We study task-specific data-free semantic segmentation, where training uses generic pretrained generative priors but has access to no target-domain images, masks, or captions--only a predefined category set. We introduce Zero-Data Semantic Segmentation (ZeroDSS), a feedback-driven approach that treats synthetic supervision as an adaptively controllable training distribution rather than a direct surrogate for real data. ZeroDSS constructs a semantically structured prompt distribution through LLM-guided compositional generation and adaptive class rebalancing, then converts the prompts into image-mask pairs using diffusion attention. Its feedback-driven distribution refinement consists of a two-phase closed-loop training procedure with a single loop-back step. In Phase I, a segmenter is trained using confidence-weighted supervision and dual-scale consistency. In Phase II, model feedback is used to adaptively target underperforming categories and refine diffusion-derived masks using model predictions. After this refined initial training, a teacher-student framework is utilized in the final phase to iteratively improve the fused supervision and segmenter through exponential moving average (EMA) updates. Using synthetic training data only, ZeroDSS achieves 35.0% mIoU on MS COCO with DeepLabV3, and 66.3% and 63.5% mIoU on PASCAL VOC with DeepLabV3 and Mask2Former, respectively. These results show that explicitly constructing and iteratively refining the synthetic supervision distribution can substantially reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in dense prediction.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Spatons: Spatiotonally Localized Building Blocks for Efficient XR Predistortion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present Spatons, a family of compositional, spatially localized neural operators for computationally efficient XR (extended reality) predistortion and distortion compensation. XR displays (AR, VR, and MR) suffer from spatial (e.g., geometric) and tonal (e.g., colour) distortions. Frames can be pre-distorted so that the projected image looks as intended. Distortions vary with manufacturing tolerances and projection systems, motivating programmable compensation. Untethered, battery-operated XR systems also require low energy and latency. A Spaton is a hybrid patch-to-pixel block combining tiny Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with fixed-function interpolation. Using Spatons, we build programmable, computationally efficient pipelines for varied distortion scenarios. On the full spatiotonal Scenario 5, Sequential-5' matches CompenNet++ in SSIM (0.944 vs. 0.944) and closely matches its PSNR (27.5 vs. 27.7 dB), with substantially lower complexity. We demonstrate a flexible Spaton solution with 6 times fewer FLOPs and 106 times fewer parameters than CompenNet++, and 4-10 times fewer memory transfers than UNet++. We characterize software implementations and analytical hardware estimates, including optimizations across target XR platforms. The distortions considered are drawn mostly from see-through, near-eye displays, where the spatial light path governs local intensity and spectral response. This early systems-level exploration uses closed-form differentiable distortions and one real projector-camera capture set for training and evaluation, rather than through-the-optics measurements. Testing on a wider range of real XR devices remains future work. Chromatic dispersion (color fringes) remains the main artifact where Spatons trail monolithic baselines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Structure-Semantic Co-optimized Latent Diffusion Model for Fast Visual Anagram Synthesis
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Visual anagram is an intriguing form of art creation wherein a single image presents different conceptual interpretations under transformations such as flipping or rotation. Recent work has achieved visual anagram synthesis by leveraging pretrained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models, yet still suffers from several key limitations including computational inefficiency, suboptimal aesthetic quality, and weak semantic fidelity and expressiveness. This work focuses on generating visual anagrams with substantially improved visual quality at minimal computational cost, thereby advancing intelligent creation of illusionary digital art. To increase image resolution while reducing time overhead, we adapt the cutting-edge parallel denoising algorithm from pixel-based T2I model to the adversarially distilled latent-based one, and accordingly propose a structure-semantic co-optimization (S2CO) framework to counteract the consequent visual degradation. As the core of our approach, S2CO framework comprises three key innovations: (\romannumeral1) null-text structure alignment optimization; (\romannumeral2) semantic enhancement optimization; (\romannumeral3) attention-guided noise fusion. Building upon these components, our method dubbed \textbf{S2CO-Anagram} is able to generate higher-resolution anagram images with noticeably superior visual harmony and semantic faithfulness than related SOTA approaches, all while achieving substantially faster inference speed. Code will be publicly available.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MSCR: Jointly Balancing Utilization Across Modalities and Discovering Synergistic Information
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross-modal interactions. Balance-oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti-dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross-modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer-based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991-collab/MSCR.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian segmentation typically binds semantic features to the per-Gaussian state via per-scene gradient training (1-4 h) or the more recent closed-form distillation. Both commit each primitive to a single feature; therefore, boundary Gaussians spanning multiple 2D instances are forced into a hard decision that degrades retrieval accuracy and yields unstable mask boundaries at render time. We present DIGS, a training-free framework with two stages, class-agnostic mapping and multi-modal encoding, that decouples instance discovery from linguistic naming. At the Gaussian level, our distribution-informed representation maintains an explicit top-$M$ label distribution per primitive, updated by a tempered Dirichlet rule; preservation of multi-peaked label distributions at boundary primitives allows a late-argmax renderer to recover clean instance boundaries. A bidirectional state machine aggregates these distributions into a persistent class-agnostic instance ontology. The instance-level encoding stage then fuses the CLIP visual embedding of each instance's isolated 3D footprint with the CLIP-text embedding of an LLM-generated attribute description, disambiguating visually similar instances. On a single A100, DIGS completes mapping and instance encoding on LERF-OVS in 1.0-3.2 min per scene, depending on whether LLM fusion is enabled, and serves native 3D queries in 5.4 ms. It reaches 71.95% mean mIoU on LERF-OVS, outperforming both the training-free SFS and training-based LaGa baselines. DIGS also achieves the highest mean mIoU on LERF-Mask and 3D-OVS and surpasses Gaga and ObjectGS on Replica under their respective evaluation protocols. Code is available at https://github.com/ZephyrZos/DIGS.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Learning from the Right Regions: Class-Conditioned Explanation Guidance for Medical Imaging
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Deep neural networks can achieve strong predictive performance in medical imaging while relying on regions unrelated to the predicted finding. Explanation-guided learning can address this problem, but multi-label classification introduces a key challenge: multiple abnormalities may coexist in an image, requiring each prediction to align with its corresponding spatial evidence. We propose a class-conditioned explanation-guided learning framework that constructs a separate explanation for each positive class and penalizes evidence outside its class-specific annotated regions. We instantiate the framework using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and evaluate it on 14 abnormalities using EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, and Swin-B. Explanation guidance substantially improves annotation alignment across all architectures: All-Saliency Precision increases from 0.140 to 0.625, 0.052 to 0.551, 0.060 to 0.403, and 0.095 to 0.570, respectively. These improvements are accompanied by smaller, architecture-dependent changes in classification performance. Our results show that class-conditioned explanation guidance can substantially improve where multi-label classifiers concentrate their explanatory evidence while largely preserving predictive performance.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Submitted to the Explainable and Trustworthy AI for Clinical Decision Support Systems Workshop, IEEE BIBM 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PACE-Mem: Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence for Multimodal Agents
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: As multimodal agents accumulate experience, their long-term memories contain many similar observations of recurring scenes, actions, and entities. Answer quality depends on the evidence retrieved from these memories into the model's context. However, query-relevant memories may contain overlapping information, and a fixed retrieval depth may return too little or too much evidence for a given question. To address these challenges, we propose PACE-Mem, Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence, which constructs a complementary evidence sequence and determines its length from the same selection trajectory. For structured memories, query-guided pooling combines records within each clip to obtain relevance scores and representations. Using these relevance scores and representations, maximal marginal relevance (MMR) selection balances query relevance against overlap with previously selected evidence. From the resulting score trajectory, a prefix-length selection algorithm determines retrieval depth by comparing length-normalized adjacent declines, accounting for both score changes and the amount of evidence accumulated. PACE-Mem is a training-free, plug-in retrieval method for clip-based agent memory systems, leaving memory construction and answer generation unchanged. Across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks, PACE-Mem improves question-answering accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k, the strongest baseline at comparable mean retrieval depths. Further analysis reveals that jointly adding and removing evidence is associated with larger net accuracy gains than either change alone.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Multimodal Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Vision-Language Models via Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Resource-exhaustion attacks against autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) typically assume unimodal threat models, treating the image branch as the primary optimization surface while holding user-visible prompts fixed. Even recent loop-centric variants remain confined to this single-channel paradigm, leaving the exploitation of availability unexplored as a cross-modal optimization problem over jointly controllable input surfaces.
  We introduce Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization (JPPO), the first compound adversarial framework elevating the visible prompt to a first-class adversarial variable alongside image perturbations. Under a restricted joint-input threat model, JPPO performs coupled, stagewise optimization over both the pixel and prompt surfaces. This produces synergistic cost amplification, mechanistically distinct from loop-dependent failures, exhibiting negligible loop incidence in our experiments.
  Evaluating five open-source VLM families on MS COCO and ImageNet under an 8/255 infinity-norm budget, JPPO achieves over 4.6x latency and 5.3x energy amplification on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and over 36.6x latency with 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2. This represents the strongest cost amplification among directly compared baselines while requiring substantially fewer optimization iterations. Ablations confirm this amplification arises from multimodal coordination rather than prompt length or isolated modalities. These findings reveal structural blind spots in current VLM serving defenses, motivating cost-aware robustness evaluation as a first-class security requirement for multimodal deployments.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted by ACM CCS 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ULTRA: Unified Multimodal Control for Autonomous Humanoid Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Achieving autonomous and versatile whole-body loco-manipulation remains a central barrier to making humanoids practically useful. Yet existing approaches are fundamentally constrained: retargeted data are often scarce or low-quality; methods struggle to scale to large skill repertoires; and, most importantly, they rely on tracking predefined motion references rather than generating behavior from perception and high-level task specifications. To address these limitations, we propose ULTRA, a unified framework with two key components. First, we introduce a physics-driven neural retargeting algorithm that translates large-scale motion capture to humanoid embodiments while preserving physical plausibility for contact-rich interactions. Second, we learn a unified multimodal controller that supports both dense references and sparse task specifications, under sensing ranging from accurate motion-capture state to noisy egocentric visual inputs. We distill a universal tracking policy into this controller, compress motor skills into a compact latent space, and apply reinforcement learning finetuning to expand coverage and improve robustness under out-of-distribution scenarios. This enables coordinated whole-body behavior from sparse intent without test-time reference motions. We evaluate ULTRA in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Results show that ULTRA generalizes to autonomous, goal-conditioned whole-body loco-manipulation from egocentric perception, consistently outperforming tracking-only baselines with limited skills.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: IROS 2026 Best Mobile Manipulation Paper Award Finalist, Project Page: https://ultrahumanoid.github.io/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: GazeAgent: VLM-Guided Implicit Gaze Calibration from Egocentric Multimodal Behavior for AI Glasses
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: AI glasses typically require explicit, user-specific eye-tracker calibration, and accuracy can drift when the device shifts during use. We present GazeAgent, a VLM-guided framework that continuously and adaptively improves gaze-calibration accuracy from naturally occurring behavior without asking users to interrupt their activities. GazeAgent identifies precise visual attention (PVA) events from multimodal streams of inertial measurement unit (IMU), gaze, and wearer-hand signals, validates their task relevance, and localizes functional targets as pseudo-calibration targets. In a 10-participant scripted study, the system detected all 820 predefined PVA opportunities and, under device disturbance, reduced median gaze error by 44.1% compared with explicit calibration. In a five-participant case study, autonomous calibration produced the lowest workload and interruption ratings, and all participants preferred it for routine use. By deriving task-critical targets from natural multimodal behavior, GazeAgent demonstrates the potential for continuous, adaptive, and low-burden gaze interaction on egocentric AI glasses.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Hexagonal Basis Projectors for Model-Based Iterative CT Reconstruction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image representation affects both the forward model and quantitative feature recovery in model-based iterative CT reconstruction. For isotropically bandlimited signals, the hexagonal lattice is the most sampling-efficient lattice in two dimensions, with greater directional isotropy and a larger alias-free bandwidth than the Cartesian grid at equal density. We develop constant and linear hexagonal projectors for two-dimensional fan-beam CT using box spline calculus. Both bases form a partition of unity on common coefficient centers; the linear tent also reproduces affine functions. We derive analytic ray footprints and effective detector-blur expressions and implement efficient GPU forward and backprojection. On simulated FORBILD data, the linear model improves on Cartesian and hexagonal pixels, with its best noisy-data accuracy at the coarser resolution. Real-world 2DeteCT comparisons use high-dose, high-resolution Cartesian reconstructions as pseudo ground truth and show competitive image and feature agreement. These results establish a practical hexagonal representation for quantitative CT.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Rate as a Feature, Not a Nuisance: Curriculum FiLM Training for Event-Based Graph Neural Networks
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: An event camera emits events at a rate given by the scene motion, object texture, illumination, its own contrast thresholds, and other settings. Across the N-Caltech101 dataset, recorded by a single event camera, the event rate varies by roughly 26x. Standard event-based Graph Neural Network GNN pipelines do not make use of the variable event rate. They either normalize each event's timestamp into a fixed window or train the network to be invariant to the event rate. We argue that both choices lose information that could instead be used to improve the performance of a pipeline. Per-recording normalization is non-invertible, incurring about 6pp (percentage points) of natural-rate accuracy loss in our setting. And invariance training trades accuracy for robustness to shifts in the event rate. We instead take a different path and condition on the event rate directly. We add a per-recording log-rate scalar that modulates every stage of a PointNet++ backbone through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), initialized to identity, so that training begins at the unmodified baseline. A two-stage curriculum (natural event rates first, then rate-augmented fine-tuning) reaches 67.2% on N-Caltech101 (+6.3pp) and 82.5% on DVS128 Gesture (+14.0pp) with an additional ~0.2M parameters. A matched-capacity control experiment shows that the gain is not from the increase in model capacity but from the rate conditioning. We will make the implementation publicly available upon acceptance of this work.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SuperClip Pyramid for Video Temporal Grounding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CaMeWM: A Causal Medical World Model for Generative Tumor Evolution and Treatment Planning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Treatment planning is intrinsically counterfactual: clinicians must compare how a patient's tumor and survival would evolve under competing regimens, whereas a retrospective cohort records only the regimen received and one follow-up scan. A treatment-conditioned generator trained on such data can therefore reproduce historical treatment allocation rather than simulate the interventional disease dynamics needed to rank regimens. We introduce \textbf{CaMeWM}, a causal medical world model for supported post-TACE tumor evolution and treatment planning. CaMeWM implements one intervention-to-decision loop rather than three independent prediction tasks: it first admits a queried regimen only for clinically comparable histories with empirical treatment support; it then generates a distribution of lesion-local follow-up worlds through an action-conditioned response descriptor, deterministic anchor, and residual 3D diffusion transition; and it finally maps sampled worlds to restricted mean survival time (RMST) with a response-Cox utility model. Under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, this loop estimates a prespecified, support-restricted g-formula target; all selection and nuisance estimation are fold-local, and the induced policy is evaluated by cross-fitted, censoring-adjusted doubly robust estimation. Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, CaMeWM achieves 0.618 SSIM and 0.528 change-map SSIM for follow-up CT transition, while its generated-world survival pathway attains a 0.615 C-index; factual-only AIPW estimates a 9.60-week RMST gain (95\% CI 0.61--18.13) for the frozen policy. CaMeWM provides an inspectable basis for retrospective, support-restricted treatment planning.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Controllable Multi-Object Insertion for Detection Data Augmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Controllable object insertion provides a targeted approach to augmenting object detection datasets that require category--count fidelity, annotation alignment, and source-content preservation beyond visual realism. Several approaches have been proposed to address this grand challenge, but most suffer from different constraints in precise category--count requests and visual consistency, limited coordination across categories and instances, and poor localization of multiple objects of specific category and count. We design SceneP2F, a two-stage trainable framework that connects scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation leveraging explicit instance-level layouts. SceneP2F consists of two novel designs. The first is ScenePlan which allocates one class-labeled query per requested instance, jointly predicts scene-compatible object centers, and separately estimates box sizes conditioned on the planned centers and scene context. The second is SceneAlign-Fill which combines geometry- and appearance-aware conditioning, box--class-guided regional attention, and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to render the planned objects while limiting unintended changes to source content. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K show that SceneP2F outperforms representative general-purpose editors and object-insertion methods consistently, demonstrating the value of coordinating instance-level planning and generation for category-targeted detection augmentation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Codec-Compatible Learned Compression for 3D Gaussian Splatting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) compression methods provide a practical route by representing Gaussian attributes as 2D maps and coding them with standard video codecs. Among these maps, high-dimensional non-DC spherical harmonics (SH-AC) maps contain the largest number of channels and account for a dominant portion of the bitstream. However, their statistics differ substantially from those of natural images, and the nonlinear dependencies among SH-AC coefficients remain insufficiently exploited. To address these issues, we propose CCT-GS, a Codec-Compatible learned Transform framework for 3DGS compression. CCT-GS first learns a generalized SH-AC transform that captures cross-scene regularities and converts SH-AC maps into compact codec-friendly bottleneck maps. It further introduces LoRA-based scene adaptation to recover scene-specific appearance details with lightweight side information. Experiments on MPEG GSC sequences demonstrate that CCT-GS consistently outperforms representative video-based baselines, achieving an average BD-rate reduction of 51.30% over the video-based anchor.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing (VCIP 2026). 5 pages, 3 figures, and 1 table

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training for Long-Video Understanding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Uncertainty Gates the Gradient: Adaptive Updates for Generalized Few-Shot 3D Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones. Complementing this, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) to enforce learning from high-confidence dense signals. On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ (1-/5-shot), UGA sets new state of the art with an average +3.08 HM IoU over the strongest prior baseline.

Machine Learning.title: CARTA: Self-Supervised Reusable Transaction Embeddings via Heterogeneous Tokenization and Cross-Attention
Machine Learning.summary: Acquiring fraud labels for payment transactions is expensive and inconsistent across tasks, and high-cardinality identifiers such as merchant names make one-hot feature pipelines infeasible at scale. We present CARTA, a self-supervised encoder that learns a compact 16-dim embedding from raw transactions without labels; the frozen embedding is then reused for label-efficient fraud probing and exploratory unsupervised risk stratification without retraining the encoder. CARTA uses type-specific projections with learned embedding tables for high-cardinality identifiers, trained with token excision and InfoNCE contrastive loss. On IEEE-CIS, its linear probe at 1% of labels exceeds a raw-feature probe at 100%; on IBM TabFormer (2M rows), its frozen embedding reaches GBDT AUPRC 0.508, above frequency encoding (0.411) and the merchant-dropping baseline (0.022), though fully-supervised CatBoost is stronger. CARTA is a label-free, reusable representation that complements task-specific supervised models.
Machine Learning.comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at ICAIF '26 (7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance), Milan, Italy, November 14-17, 2026

Machine Learning.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design
Machine Learning.summary: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.

Machine Learning.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
Machine Learning.summary:
Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives.
  We present \textsc{ATLAS}, an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. \textsc{ATLAS} uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed \textsc{ATLAS} for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. \textsc{ATLAS} achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of $87.4\%$, exceeding mean baseline accuracy by $26.4$ percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0\% downtime.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (ATC 2026)

Machine Learning.title: A Symmetry-Matching Approach to Blind-Spot Reduction in Sparse Autoencoders
Machine Learning.summary: Language models can treat semantically distinct inputs as interchangeable at the representation level, creating blind spots that standard sparse autoencoder (SAE) objectives do not target. In safety-critical settings such as clinical dosage extraction, legal clause interpretation, or financial amount verification, such failures can propagate silently into downstream decisions. We study this problem as one of feature-basis orientation. Building on a symmetry-matching view from algebraic error-detection theory, we add a differentiable $V_{\mathrm{Gini}}$ regularisation term to SAE training that penalises uneven perturbation response within a specified family. Across GPT-2, Gemma 2, and Qwen 2.5, a frozen multi-seed evaluation shows that $V$-regularisation raises both relative and absolute lower-tail responses while reducing response-profile imbalance, with no material general-text reconstruction degradation. JumpReLU and minimum description length (MDL) objectives remain close to the Standard SAE profile under the same protocol. Family-geometry controls show that the effect is not explained by template duplication or a single dominant perturbation family, and held-out probes plus null-calibrated separation tests evaluate how far the representation-level change carries to downstream discriminability. A zero-shot audit on out-of-distribution clinical radiology minimal pairs finds the relative weak-tail lift in all evaluated model-by-family cells, not perfectly rank-aligned with the trained statistic, and a held-out family audit finds it on family kinds never used in training. Together, the results show that perturbation-aware SAE training can reorient feature bases toward safety-relevant input changes while leaving downstream validation as a separate empirical step.

Machine Learning.title: Distribution-Based Regularization for Reward Fine-Tuning Diffusion and Flow Models
Machine Learning.summary: Reward fine-tuning is an effective way to adapt pretrained diffusion and flow-matching models to downstream objectives, but aggressive optimization often leads to mode collapse and distributional drift. Existing methods attempt to control this drift with reverse-KL regularization, implemented as an $\ell_2$ penalty on the velocity field; however, this functions by indirectly constraining sampling dynamics rather than directly acting on the generated distribution. To address this, we propose DFR (Distributional Functional Rewards), which augments the task reward with a distribution-dependent, per-sample reward that acts explicitly on the generated distribution. Formally, we generalize the KL-regularized objective from expected rewards, which are linear in the model's distribution, to convex functionals of it. The first variation of this objective defines an effective, distribution-dependent reward that directly penalizes deviation from the pretrained distribution. This formulation yields additive per-sample rewards for the Fréchet distance (FD), maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and DreamSim diversity, recovering several recently proposed rewards as special cases. Across various text-to-image fine-tuning tasks, DFR matches the peak reward of KL-tuned baselines while increasing diversity by up to 29% at equal or lower drift.

Machine Learning.title: LastWords: Boring Problems Revisited
Machine Learning.summary: In 2022, the second author published a Last Words piece in Computational Linguistics in which he pointed out that, despite the advances in AI up to that point, there were still some problems in natural language processing that on the one hand seemed trivial and perhaps boring, but on the other were hard to solve using purely neural methods. One such problem discussed in that context was text normalization, and a particular subproblem of that, namely number name reading. The piece came out just a few months before the first release of ChatGPT, and needless to say, a lot has happened since then. Indeed, as we document here, the problem (of number name reading) has practically been solved, at least by one of the latest frontier models. However, we believe that there are still open issues for such limited domain, constrained and limited resource problems, and that in some future machine learning approach, the massive resources of the latest frontier models would not be needed to solve them.

Machine Learning.title: Statistical Inference and Learning for Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)
Machine Learning.summary:
The SHAP (short for Shapley additive explanation) framework has become an essential tool for attributing importance to variables in predictive tasks. In model-agnostic settings, SHAP uses the concept of Shapley values from cooperative game theory to fairly allocate credit to the features in a vector $X$ based on their contribution to an outcome $Y$. While the explanations offered by SHAP are local by nature, learners often need global measures of feature importance in order to improve model explainability and perform feature selection. The most common approach for converting these local explanations into global ones is to compute either the mean absolute SHAP or mean squared SHAP. However, despite their ubiquity, there do not exist approaches for performing statistical inference on these quantities.
  In this paper, we take a semi-parametric approach for calibrating confidence in estimates of the $p$th powers of Shapley additive explanations. We show that, by treating the SHAP curve as a nuisance function that must be estimated from data, one can reliably construct asymptotically normal estimates of the $p$th powers of SHAP. When $p \geq 2$, we show a de-biased estimator that combines U-statistics with Neyman orthogonal scores for functionals of nested regressions is asymptotically normal. When $1 \leq p < 2$ (and the hence target parameter is not twice differentiable), we construct de-biased U-statistics for a smoothed alternative. In particular, we show how to carefully tune the temperature parameter of the smoothing function in order to obtain inference for the true, unsmoothed $p$th power. We complement these results by presenting a Neyman orthogonal loss that can be used to learn the SHAP curve via empirical risk minimization and discussing excess risk guarantees for commonly used function classes.

Machine Learning.title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
Machine Learning.summary: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling. Our perturbation analysis separates the effects of distribution-level sampling, finite within-bag sampling, and random feature approximation. We establish sufficient feature-budget conditions under which RaDR preserves the order of our excess-risk upper bound for exact two-stage kernel distribution regression while maintaining computational efficiency. We further propose Adaptive Random Feature Distribution Regression (A-RaDR), a unified score-guided framework that adaptively allocates random features according to downstream learning objectives. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets demonstrate that RaDR delivers substantial computational savings while maintaining competitive predictive performance, whereas A-RaDR further improves learning accuracy in distribution regression while retaining the computational speed up. Together, these results establish a practical and theoretically grounded framework for adaptive, scalable distribution learning

Machine Learning.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Topology optimization places material in a design domain to optimize a structure's performance, such as its stiffness or heat conduction. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a lower-quality learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Replacing the classical code with an efficient implementation of the same algorithm cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we picked this point after the runs, which gives the classical code its best case. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed, and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.
Machine Learning.comment: 32 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Research article: tests of released code for eight topology-optimization methods and an exploratory audit of published speed claims

Machine Learning.title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
Machine Learning.summary:
We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness.
  First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020].
  Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(π+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $π/2$ in the leading constant.

Machine Learning.title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
Machine Learning.summary: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main). Code and data: https://github.com/nlpsoc/EmbDivBench

Machine Learning.title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with General Utilities via Neural Dual Critics
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning with general utilities optimizes nonlinear functionals of policy-induced occupancy measures. We develop a natural actor-critic method for concave RLGU objectives admitting an exact variational dual representation, with explicit constructions for a broad class of separable occupancy utilities. Rather than estimating the occupancy measure and then forming the policy-gradient pseudo-reward, our method learns this pseudo-reward directly as a function of the state-action pair using a neural critic. The critic is trained by projected stochastic updates, while multilevel Monte Carlo combines outputs across training horizons to control its bias at logarithmic expected cost. Our analysis separates conditional actor bias from estimator second moments and accounts explicitly for dual optimization, critic approximation, and neural linearization errors. Under policy-transfer, dual-stability, and local critic-regularity conditions, the method achieves $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ global convergence above policy, critic-class, and finite-width approximation errors using $\widetilde{O}(T)$ expected environment transitions and reference samples. For a fixed critic representation, this yields $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sampling complexity above the approximation floor, covering infinite state-action spaces and occupancy utilities beyond fixed finite vectors of returns.

Machine Learning.title: RAFT: Redundancy-Aware Input Filtering for Temporal Graph Neural Network Training
Machine Learning.summary: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have shown strong performance on dynamic graph learning tasks by continuously updating node memories from evolving interactions (i.e., events) and leveraging these memories for downstream predictions. As graphs grow rapidly in modern applications, training requires processing an increasing number of events; meanwhile, each event can update node memories used by later events, creating dependencies that constrain parallel execution and limit the benefits of additional computing resources. These costs motivate an upstream question: Are all events, and the dependencies they introduce, necessary for learning? We investigate this question through two roles of temporal events: prediction targets and historical events sampled as inputs. We observe that targets involving stable node memories tend to exhibit lower prediction loss, while filtering historical events associated with stable memories can retain similar training-loss trajectories in several evaluated settings. Together, these observations suggest an opportunity to identify input redundancy through changes in node memories. Building on this opportunity, we propose RAFT, a redundancy-aware input-filtering framework for TGNN training. RAFT tracks memory changes during training and uses them to guide two filters: a root-event filter removes selected prediction targets before training, and a support-event filter excludes selected historical context during sampling. Filtering inputs before their downstream preparation and processing reduces the work they trigger. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%, while reducing recorded training time by up to 52.56\% with negligible changes to model precisions.

Machine Learning.title: Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs
Machine Learning.summary: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

Machine Learning.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
Machine Learning.summary: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.
Machine Learning.comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 17 tables. Code and labels: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/missing-compliance-class-4F6F

Machine Learning.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
Machine Learning.summary:
A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state.
  On $τ^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

Machine Learning.title: FlowMaker: From Tasks to Cost-Efficient Generative AI Workflow Deployments
Machine Learning.summary: Generative AI workflows execute user tasks by composing sequences of LLM calls, where each call performs a sub-task (e.g., summarization or translation), forming a workflow. Executing such workflows requires decisions over workflow structure, model assignments, and deployment configurations, which jointly determine latency, cost, and accuracy under dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Existing systems optimize these decisions in isolation or fix them early, leading to suboptimal cost and goodput. We make two key observations. First, efficient serving requires jointly exploring all combinations of workflows, model choices, and deployment configurations under dynamic cluster state. Second, reuse of deployed LLMs is critical for reducing cost, but must be performed on-the-fly, as reuse depends on current load and resource availability. Together, these make selecting a workflow-variant-a combination of workflow, models, and deployment configuration-a time-critical problem. We present FlowMaker, which exposes a task-level interface and selects workflow-variants on behalf of users. To realize this, we design a constraint-guided load-aware pruning algorithm for fast, on-the-fly decisions. FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14$\times$ and reduces cost by up to 2.77$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including Murakkab.

Machine Learning.title: The Dichotomy Between Pattern Recognition and Step-by-Step Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary: We argue that pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning are two ends of a spectrum. A large language model (LLM) learns to reason step-by-step when data is structured such that the next token depends on a small amount of preceding context.
